To You!

The aim of this book is the salvation of the reader. The one who spoke and wrote it will be greatly disappointed if it does not lead many to the Lord Jesus. It is sent out in childlike dependence on the power of God the Holy Spirit, to use it in the conversion of millions, if he pleases. No doubt many poor men and women will pick up this little book, and the Lord will visit them with grace. With them in mind, the plainest language has been chosen, and many everyday expressions have been used. But if the wealthy and well-placed should glance at this book, the Holy Spirit can reach them too; for what the uneducated can understand is no less appealing to the educated. Oh, that some who read it might become great winners of souls!

Who knows how many will find their way to peace through what they read here? A more important question for you, dear reader, is this — Will you be one of them?

A certain man placed a fountain by the wayside, and he hung up a cup next to it on a little chain. Some time later he was told that a great art critic had found much fault with its design. “But,” he said, “do many thirsty people drink at it?” Then they told him that thousands of poor people, men, women, and children, quenched their thirst at this fountain; and he smiled and said that the critic’s remark did not trouble him much, only he hoped that on some hot summer’s day the critic himself might fill the cup, and be refreshed, and praise the name of the Lord.

Here is my fountain, and here is my cup: find fault if you like; but do drink the water of life. This is all I care about. I would rather bless the soul of the poorest street sweeper or rag collector than please a royal prince and fail to convert him to God.

Reader, do you mean business in reading these pages? If so, we are agreed from the start; but nothing short of your finding Christ and heaven is what this book aims at. Oh, that we may seek this together! I do so by dedicating this little book in prayer. Will you not join me by looking up to God and asking him to bless you while you read? Providence has put these pages in your way, you have a little spare time in which to read them, and you feel willing to give them your attention. These are good signs. Who knows? Perhaps the time God has set for blessing you has come. At any rate, “The Holy Spirit says, ‘Today, if you+ hear His voice, do not harden your+ hearts.’”

What Are We Aiming At?

I heard a story; I think it came from the north of England. A minister called on a poor woman, meaning to give her help, for he knew that she was very poor. With his money in his hand, he knocked at the door; but she did not answer. He concluded she was not at home, and went on his way. A little later he met her at church, and told her that he had remembered her need: “I called at your house, and knocked several times, and I suppose you were not at home, for I had no answer.” “What time did you call, sir?” “It was about noon.” “Oh, dear,” she said, “I heard you, sir, and I am so sorry I did not answer; but I thought it was the man calling for the rent.” Many a poor woman knows what this meant. Now, I want to be heard, and so I must say that I am not calling for the rent; indeed, the aim of this book is not to ask anything of you, but to tell you that salvation is all of grace, which means, free, gratis, for nothing.

Often, when we are anxious to win attention, our hearer thinks, “Ah! Now I am going to be told my duty. It is the man calling for what is owed to God, and I am sure I have nothing to pay with. I will not be at home.” No, this book does not come to make a demand on you, but to bring you something. We are not going to talk about law, and duty, and punishment, but about love, and goodness, and forgiveness, and mercy, and eternal life. So do not act as if you were not at home: do not turn a deaf ear, or a careless heart. I am asking nothing of you in the name of God or man. I do not intend to require anything of you; but I come in God’s name to bring you a free gift, which it will be your present and eternal joy to receive. Open the door, and let my pleading come in. “Come now, let us reason together.” The Lord himself invites you to talk with him about your immediate and endless happiness, and he would not have done this if he did not mean you well. Do not refuse the Lord Jesus who knocks at your door; for he knocks with a hand that was nailed to the tree for people like you. Since his one and only aim is your good, incline your ear and come to him. Listen carefully, and let the good word sink into your soul. It may be that the hour has come in which you will enter on that new life which is the beginning of heaven. Faith comes by hearing, and reading is a kind of hearing: faith may come to you while you are reading this book. Why not? O blessed Spirit of all grace, make it so!

God Justifies The Ungodly

Listen to a little sermon. You will find the text in the Epistle to the Romans, in the fourth chapter and the fifth verse:

““To the one who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness.””

I want to draw your attention to those words, “Him who justifies the ungodly.” They seem to me very wonderful words.

Are you not surprised that there should be such an expression as that in the Bible, “Who justifies the ungodly”? I have heard that men who hate the doctrines of the cross bring it as a charge against God that he saves wicked men and receives to himself the vilest of the vile. See how this Scripture accepts the charge and plainly states it! By the mouth of his servant Paul, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, he takes to himself the title of “Him who justifies the ungodly.” He makes those just who are unjust, forgives those who deserve to be punished, and favors those who deserve no favor. You thought, did you not, that salvation was for the good? That God’s grace was for the pure and holy, who are free from sin? It has come into your head that if you were excellent, then God would reward you; and you have thought that because you are not worthy, there could be no way for you to enjoy his favor. You must be somewhat surprised to read a text like this: “Him who justifies the ungodly.” I do not wonder that you are surprised; for with all my familiarity with the great grace of God, I never stop wondering at it. It does sound surprising, does it not, that it should be possible for a holy God to justify an unholy man? We, following the natural legalism of our hearts, are always talking about our own goodness and our own worthiness, and we stubbornly insist that there must be something in us to win God’s notice. Now God, who sees through all deceptions, knows that there is no goodness whatever in us. He says that “there is no one righteous, not even one.” He knows that “all our righteous acts are like filthy rags”; and therefore the Lord Jesus did not come into the world to look for goodness and righteousness among men, but to bring goodness and righteousness with him and give them to people who have none of them. He comes, not because we are just, but to make us so: he justifies the ungodly.

When a counselor comes into court, if he is an honest man, he wants to plead the case of an innocent person and justify him before the court when charges are falsely laid against him. It should be the lawyer’s aim to justify the innocent person, and he should not try to shield the guilty party. It does not lie in man’s right nor in man’s power truly to justify the guilty. This is a miracle reserved for the Lord alone. God, the infinitely just Sovereign, knows that there is not a just man on earth who does good and does not sin, and therefore, in the infinite sovereignty of his divine nature and in the splendor of his inexpressible love, he undertakes the task, not so much of justifying the just as of justifying the ungodly. God has devised ways and means of making the ungodly man stand justly accepted before him: he has set up a system by which, with perfect justice, he can treat the guilty man as if he had been free from offense all his life, yes, can treat him as if he were wholly free from sin. He justifies the ungodly.

Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners. It is a very surprising thing — a thing to be marveled at most of all by those who enjoy it. I know that to me, even to this day, it is the greatest wonder I ever heard of, that God should ever justify me. I feel myself to be a lump of unworthiness, a mass of corruption, and a heap of sin, apart from his almighty love. I know with full assurance that I am justified by faith which is in Christ Jesus, and treated as if I had been perfectly just, and made an heir of God and a joint-heir with Christ; and yet by nature I must take my place among the most sinful. I, who am altogether undeserving, am treated as if I had been deserving. I am loved with as much love as if I had always been godly, whereas before I was ungodly. Who can help being astonished at this? Gratitude for such favor stands dressed in robes of wonder.

Now, while this is very surprising, I want you to notice how available it makes the gospel to you and to me. If God justifies the ungodly, then, dear friend, he can justify you. Is that not the very kind of person you are? If you are unconverted at this moment, it describes you exactly: you have lived without God, you have been the reverse of godly; in one word, you have been and are ungodly. Perhaps you have not even gone to a place of worship on the Sabbath, but have lived in disregard of God’s day, and house, and Word — this proves you to have been ungodly. Sadder still, it may be that you have even tried to doubt God’s existence, and have gone so far as to say that you did. You have lived on this fair earth, which is full of the signs of God’s presence, and all the while you have shut your eyes to the clear evidence of his power and Godhead. You have lived as if there were no God. Indeed, you would have been very pleased if you could have proved to yourself for certain that there was no God at all. Possibly you have lived a great many years in this way, so that you are now pretty well settled in your ways, and yet God is not in any of them. If you were labeled ungodly, it would describe you as well as the label salt water would describe the sea. Would it not?

Or perhaps you are a person of another sort; you have regularly kept all the outward forms of religion, and yet you have had no heart in them at all, but have really been ungodly. Though meeting with the people of God, you have never met with God for yourself; you have been in the choir, and yet have not praised the Lord with your heart. You have lived without any love for God in your heart, or regard for his commands in your life. Well, you are just the kind of man to whom this gospel is sent — this gospel which says that God justifies the ungodly. It is very wonderful, but it is happily available for you. It just suits you. Does it not? How I wish that you would accept it! If you are a sensible man, you will see the remarkable grace of God in providing for people like you, and you will say to yourself, “Justify the ungodly! Why, then, should I not be justified, and justified at once?”

Now, notice further that it must be so — that the salvation of God is for those who do not deserve it and have no preparation for it. It is reasonable that the statement should be put in the Bible; for, dear friend, no one needs justifying except those who have no justification of their own. If any of my readers are perfectly righteous, they need no justifying. You feel that you are doing your duty well, and almost putting heaven in your debt. What do you want with a Savior, or with mercy? What do you want with justification? You will be tired of my book by this time, for it will hold no interest for you.

If any of you+ are giving yourselves+ such proud airs, listen to me for a little while. You+ will be lost, as sure as you+ are alive. You+ righteous men, whose righteousness is all of your+ own working, are either deceivers or deceived; for the Scripture cannot lie, and it says plainly, “There is no one righteous, not even one.” In any case I have no gospel to preach to the self-righteous — no, not a word of it. Jesus Christ himself did not come to call the righteous, and I am not going to do what he did not do. If I called you+, you+ would not come, and so I will not call you+ as righteous. No, I urge you+ instead to look at that righteousness of yours+ till you+ see what a delusion it is. It is not half as substantial as a cobweb. Be done with it! Flee from it! O friends, the only people who can need justification are those who are not just in themselves. They need something to be done for them to make them just before the judgment seat of God. Depend on it, the Lord does only what is needful. Infinite wisdom never attempts what is unnecessary. Jesus never undertakes what is superfluous. To make him just who is just is no work for God — that would be a labor for a fool; but to make him just who is unjust — that is work for infinite love and mercy. To justify the ungodly — this is a miracle worthy of a God. And it certainly is so.

Now, look. If there is anywhere in the world a physician who has discovered sure and precious remedies, to whom is that physician sent? To those who are perfectly healthy? I think not. Put him down in a district where there are no sick people, and he feels that he is out of place. There is nothing for him to do. “It is not the healthy who need a physician, but the sick.” Is it not equally clear that the great remedies of grace and redemption are for the sick in soul? They cannot be for the healthy, for they can be of no use to them. If you, dear friend, feel that you are spiritually sick, the Physician has come into the world for you. If you are altogether ruined by your sin, you are the very person the plan of salvation aims at. I say that the Lord of love had just such people as you in his eye when he arranged the system of grace. Suppose a man of generous spirit were to resolve to forgive all those who were in debt to him; clearly this can only apply to those really in his debt. One person owes him a thousand dollars; another owes him fifty dollars; each one has only to have his bill marked paid, and the debt is wiped out. But the most generous person cannot forgive the debts of those who do not owe him anything. It is out of the power of omnipotence to forgive where there is no sin. Pardon, therefore, cannot be for you who have no sin. Pardon must be for the guilty. Forgiveness must be for the sinful. It would be absurd to talk of forgiving those who do not need forgiveness — pardoning those who have never offended.

Do you think that you must be lost because you are a sinner? That is the very reason why you can be saved. Because you acknowledge yourself to be a sinner, I would encourage you to believe that grace is ordained for people like you. One of our hymn writers even dared to say—

““A sinner is a sacred thing;

The Holy Ghost hath made him so.””

It is really true that Jesus seeks and saves what is lost. He died and made a real atonement for real sinners. When men are not playing with words, or calling themselves “miserable sinners” out of mere compliment, I am overjoyed to meet them. I would be glad to talk all night to bona fide sinners. The inn of mercy never closes its doors on such people, on weekdays or on Sundays. Our Lord Jesus did not die for imaginary sins, but his heart’s blood was spilled to wash out deep crimson stains, which nothing else can remove.

The sinner black with sin — he is the kind of man that Jesus Christ came to make white. A gospel preacher once preached a sermon on “The ax lies ready at the root of the trees”; and he preached such a sermon that one of his hearers said to him, “One would have thought you had been preaching to criminals. Your sermon ought to have been given in the county jail.” “Oh, no,” said the good man, “if I were preaching in the county jail, I would not preach from that text. There I would preach, ‘This is a faithful saying, and worthy of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.’” Just so. The law is for the self-righteous, to humble their pride: the gospel is for the lost, to remove their despair.

If you are not lost, what do you want with a Savior? Should the shepherd go after those who never went astray? Why should the woman sweep her house for coins that were never out of her purse? No, the medicine is for the diseased; the giving of life is for the dead; the pardon is for the guilty; liberation is for those who are bound; the opening of eyes is for those who are blind. How can the Savior, and his death on the cross, and the gospel of pardon, be accounted for, unless we suppose that men are guilty and deserve condemnation? The sinner is the gospel’s reason for existing. You, my friend, to whom this word now comes, if you are undeserving, ill-deserving, hell-deserving, you are the sort of man for whom the gospel is ordained, and arranged, and proclaimed. God justifies the ungodly.

I would like to make this very plain. I hope that I have done so already; but still, plain as it is, only the Lord can make a man see it. At first it does seem most amazing to an awakened man that salvation should really be for him as a lost and guilty one. He thinks that it must be for him as a penitent man, forgetting that his penitence is a part of his salvation. “Oh,” he says, “but I must be this and that” — all of which is true, for he will be this and that as the result of salvation; but salvation comes to him before he has any of the results of salvation. It comes to him, in fact, while he deserves only this bare, beggarly, base, abominable description, “ungodly.” That is all he is when God’s gospel comes to justify him.

May I, therefore, urge any who have no good thing about them — who fear that they have not even a good feeling, or anything at all that can recommend them to God — to believe firmly that our gracious God is able and willing to take them without anything to recommend them, and to forgive them spontaneously, not because they are good, but because he is good. Does he not make his sun shine on the evil as well as on the good? Does he not give fruitful seasons, and send the rain and the sunshine in their time on the most ungodly nations? Yes, even Sodom had its sun, and Gomorrah had its dew. O friend, the great grace of God goes beyond anything I can conceive and anything you can conceive, and I want you to think of it as it deserves. As high as the heavens are above the earth, so high are God’s thoughts above our thoughts. He can abundantly pardon. Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners: forgiveness is for the guilty.

Do not try to touch yourself up and make yourself something other than you really are; but come as you are to him who justifies the ungodly. A great artist some time ago had painted some members of the council of the city in which he lived, and he wanted, for the sake of history, to include in his picture certain characters well known in the town. A street sweeper, unkempt, ragged, filthy, was known to everybody, and there was a suitable place for him in the picture. The artist said to this ragged and rugged fellow, “I will pay you well if you will come down to my studio and let me paint your portrait.” He came by in the morning, but he was soon sent on his way; for he had washed his face, and combed his hair, and put on a respectable suit of clothes. He was needed as a beggar, and was not invited in any other role. Even so, the gospel will receive you into its halls if you come as a sinner, but not otherwise. Do not wait to reform yourself, but come at once for salvation. God justifies the ungodly, and that picks you up where you now are: it meets you in your worst state.

Come in your déshabille. I mean, come to your heavenly Father in all your sin and sinfulness. Come to Jesus just as you are, leprous, filthy, naked, neither fit to live nor fit to die. Come, you who are the very sweepings of creation; come, though you hardly dare to hope for anything but death. Come, though despair is brooding over you, pressing on your chest like a horrible nightmare. Come and ask the Lord to justify another ungodly one. Why should he not? Come along, then; for this great mercy of God is meant for people like you. I put it in the words of the text, and I cannot put it more strongly: the Lord God himself takes to himself this gracious title, “Him who justifies the ungodly.” He makes just, and causes to be treated as just, those who by nature are ungodly. Is that not a wonderful word for you? Reader, do not get up from your seat till you have thought this matter through.

“It Is God Who Justifies”

“Rom 8:33.”

A wonderful thing, this being justified, or made just! If we had never broken the laws of God, we would not have needed it, for we would have been just in ourselves. The man who has all his life done the things he ought to have done, and has never done anything he ought not to have done, is justified by the law. But you, dear reader, are not of that sort, I am quite sure. You are too honest to pretend to be without sin, and therefore you need to be justified.

Now, if you justify yourself, you will simply be deceiving yourself. So do not try it. It is never worthwhile.

If you ask your fellow mortals to justify you, what can they do? You can get some of them to speak well of you for a penny, and others will speak ill of you behind your back for less than that. Their judgment is not worth much.

Our text says, “It is God who justifies,” and this is far more to the point. It is an astonishing fact, and one that we ought to consider with care. Come and see.

In the first place, nobody but God would ever have thought of justifying those who are guilty. They have lived in open rebellion; they have done evil with both hands; they have gone from bad to worse; they have turned back to sin even after they have smarted for it and have therefore been forced to leave it for a while. They have broken the law and trampled on the gospel. They have refused proclamations of mercy and have persisted in ungodliness. How can they be forgiven and justified? Their fellow men, despairing of them, say, “They are hopeless cases.” Even Christians look on them with sorrow rather than with hope. But not so their God. He, in the splendor of his electing grace, having chosen some of them before the foundation of the world, will not rest till he has justified them and made them accepted in the Beloved. Is it not written, “Those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified”? So you see there are some whom the Lord resolves to justify: why should you and I not be among them?

No one but a God would ever have thought of justifying me. I am a wonder to myself. I do not doubt that grace is seen just as clearly in others. Look at Saul of Tarsus, who foamed at the mouth against God’s servants. Like a hungry wolf, he tore into the lambs and the sheep right and left; and yet God struck him down on the road to Damascus, and changed his heart, and so fully justified him that before long this man became the greatest preacher of justification by faith who ever lived. He must often have marveled that he was justified by faith in Christ Jesus; for he was once a determined stickler for salvation by the works of the law. No one but God would ever have thought of justifying such a man as Saul the persecutor; but the Lord God is glorious in grace.

But even if anybody had thought of justifying the ungodly, no one but God could have done it. It is quite impossible for anyone to forgive offenses that have not been committed against himself. Someone has greatly injured you; you can forgive him, and I hope you will; but no third person can forgive him apart from you. If the wrong is done to you, the pardon must come from you. If we have sinned against God, it is in God’s power to forgive; for the sin is against himself. That is why David says, in the fifty-first Psalm: “Against You, You only, have I sinned and done what is evil in Your sight”; for then God, against whom the offense is committed, can put the offense away. What we owe to God, our great Creator can cancel, if he pleases; and if he cancels it, it is canceled. Only the great God, against whom we have committed the sin, can blot out that sin; let us, therefore, make sure that we go to him and seek mercy at his hands. Let us not be led astray by priests, who would have us confess to them; they have no warrant in the Word of God for their claims. But even if they were ordained to pronounce absolution in God’s name, it must still be better to go ourselves to the great Lord through Jesus Christ, the Mediator, and seek and find pardon at his hand; since we are sure that this is the right way. Religion by proxy carries too great a risk: you had better see to your soul’s affairs yourself, and leave them in no man’s hands.

Only God can justify the ungodly; but he can do it to perfection. He casts our sins behind his back; he blots them out; he says that though they are searched for, they will not be found. With no other reason for it but his own infinite goodness, he has prepared a glorious way by which he can make scarlet sins as white as snow, and remove our transgressions from us as far as the east is from the west. He says, “I will not remember your sins.” He goes so far as to make an end of sin. One of old cried out in amazement, “Who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity and passes over the transgression of the remnant of His inheritance? He does not retain His anger forever, because He delights in mercy.”

We are not now speaking of justice, nor of God’s dealing with men according to what they deserve. If you claim to deal with the righteous Lord on the terms of the law, everlasting wrath threatens you, for that is what you deserve. Blessed be his name, he has not dealt with us according to our sins; but now he deals with us on terms of free grace and infinite compassion, and he says, “I will receive you graciously, and love you freely.” Believe it, for it is certainly true that the great God is able to treat the guilty with abundant mercy; yes, he is able to treat the ungodly as if they had always been godly. Read carefully the parable of the prodigal son, and see how the forgiving father received the returning wanderer with as much love as if he had never gone away, and had never defiled himself with prostitutes. So far did he carry this that the elder brother began to grumble at it; but the father never withdrew his love. O my brother, however guilty you may be, if you will only come back to your God and Father, he will treat you as if you had never done wrong. He will regard you as just, and deal with you accordingly. What do you say to this?

Do you not see — for I want to bring out clearly what a splendid thing it is — that while no one but God would think of justifying the ungodly, and no one but God could do it, the Lord can do it? See how the apostle puts the challenge: “Who will bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies.” If God has justified a man, it is well done, it is rightly done, it is justly done, it is everlastingly done. I read the other day in a paper that is full of venom against the Gospel and those who preach it, that we hold some kind of theory by which we imagine that sin can be removed from men. We hold no theory; we proclaim a fact. The grandest fact under heaven is this — that Christ by his precious blood does actually put away sin, and that God, for Christ’s sake, dealing with men on terms of divine mercy, forgives the guilty and justifies them, not according to anything that he sees in them, or foresees will be in them, but according to the riches of his mercy which lie in his own heart. This we have preached, do preach, and will preach as long as we live. “It is God who justifies” — who justifies the ungodly; he is not ashamed of doing it, nor are we of preaching it.

The justification which comes from God himself must be beyond question. If the Judge acquits me, who can condemn me? If the highest court in the universe has pronounced me just, who will bring any charge against me? Justification from God is a sufficient answer to an awakened conscience. Through it the Holy Spirit breathes peace over our entire nature, and we are no longer afraid. With this justification we can answer all the roaring and reviling of Satan and ungodly men. With this we will be able to die: with this we will boldly rise again and face the last great judgment.

““Bold shall I stand in that great day,

For who aught to my charge shall lay?

While by my Lord absolved I am

From sin’s tremendous curse and blame.””

Friend, the Lord can blot out all your sins. This is no shot in the dark. “Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men.” Though you are steeped up to your throat in crime, he can with a word remove the defilement, and say, “I am willing. Be clean!” The Lord is a great forgiver.

“I believe in the forgiveness of sins.” Do you?

He can, this very hour, pronounce the sentence, “Your sins are forgiven; go in peace”; and if he does this, no power in heaven, or earth, or under the earth, can put you under suspicion, much less under wrath. Do not doubt the power of Almighty love. You could not forgive your fellow man if he had offended you as you have offended God; but you must not measure God’s grain with your bushel; his thoughts and ways are as much above yours as the heavens are high above the earth.

“Well,” you say, “it would be a great miracle if the Lord were to pardon me.” Just so. It would be a supreme miracle, and therefore he is likely to do it; for he does “great and unsearchable things” that we did not expect.

I was myself struck down with a horrible sense of guilt, which made my life a misery to me; but when I heard the command, “Look to Me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth, for I am God, and there is no other” — I looked, and in a moment the Lord justified me. Jesus Christ, made sin for me, was what I saw, and that sight gave me rest. When those who had been bitten by the fiery serpents in the wilderness looked to the bronze serpent, they were healed at once; and so was I when I looked to the crucified Savior. The Holy Spirit, who enabled me to believe, gave me peace through believing. I felt as sure that I was forgiven as I had felt sure of condemnation before. I had been certain of my condemnation because the word of God declared it, and my conscience bore witness to it; but when the Lord justified me, I was made equally certain by the same witnesses. The word of the Lord in Scripture says, “He who believes in Him is not condemned,” and my conscience bears witness that I believed, and that God in pardoning me is just. So I have the witness of the Holy Spirit and of my own conscience, and these two agree in one. Oh, how I wish that my reader would receive the testimony of God on this matter, and then very soon he would also have the witness in himself!

I venture to say that a sinner justified by God stands on even surer footing than a righteous man justified by his works, if there is any such man. We could never be sure that we had done enough works; conscience would always be uneasy for fear that, after all, we might fall short, and we could rely only on the trembling verdict of a fallible judgment; but when God himself justifies, and the Holy Spirit bears witness to it by giving us peace with God, why, then we feel that the matter is sure and settled, and we enter into rest. No tongue can tell the depth of that calm which comes over the soul that has received the peace of God which surpasses all understanding. Friend, do seek it at once.

Just And The Justifier

We have seen the ungodly justified, and have considered the great truth that only God can justify any man; we now go a step further and ask — How can a just God justify guilty men? Here we find a full answer in the words of Paul, in Romans 3:21 to 26. We will read six verses from the chapter so as to follow the flow of the passage:

“But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been revealed, as attested by the Law and the Prophets. And this righteousness from God comes through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe. There is no distinction, for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. God presented Him as a propitiation through faith in His blood, in order to demonstrate His righteousness, because in His forbearance He had passed over the sins committed beforehand. He did this to demonstrate His righteousness at the present time, so as to be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.”

Here let me give you a bit of personal experience. When I was under the hand of the Holy Spirit, under conviction of sin, I had a clear and sharp sense of the justice of God. Sin, whatever it might be to other people, became an unbearable burden to me. It was not so much that I feared hell, but that I feared sin. I knew myself to be so horribly guilty that I remember feeling that if God did not punish me for sin, he ought to. I felt that the Judge of all the earth ought to condemn such sin as mine. I sat on the judgment seat, and I condemned myself to perish; for I confessed that if I had been God, I could have done nothing else than send such a guilty creature as I was down to the lowest hell. All the while, I had on my mind a deep concern for the honor of God’s name and the integrity of his moral government. I felt that it would not satisfy my conscience if I could be forgiven unjustly. The sin I had committed must be punished. But then there was the question how God could be just and yet justify me, who had been so guilty. I asked my heart: “How can he be just and yet the justifier?” I was worried and wearied with this question; nor could I see any answer to it. Certainly I could never have invented an answer that would have satisfied my conscience.

The doctrine of the atonement is to my mind one of the surest proofs of the divine inspiration of Holy Scripture. Who would or could have thought of the just Ruler dying for the unjust rebel? This is no teaching of human mythology, or dream of the poetic imagination. This way of expiation is known among men only because it is a fact; fiction could not have devised it. God himself ordained it; it is not a thing that could have been imagined.

I had heard the plan of salvation by the sacrifice of Jesus from my youth; but I knew no more about it in my innermost soul than if I had been born and bred where the gospel was never heard. The light was there, but I was blind; it was necessary that the Lord himself should make the matter plain to me. It came to me as a new revelation, as fresh as if I had never read in Scripture that Jesus was declared to be the propitiation for sins so that God might be just. I believe it will have to come as a revelation to every newborn child of God whenever he sees it; I mean that glorious doctrine of the substitution of the Lord Jesus. I came to understand that salvation was possible through vicarious sacrifice, and that provision had been made in the first constitution and arrangement of things for such a substitution. I was made to see that he who is the Son of God, co-equal and co-eternal with the Father, had long ago been made the covenant head of a chosen people, so that he might in that role suffer for them and save them. Since our fall was not at first a personal one, for we fell in our federal representative, the first Adam, it became possible for us to be restored by a second representative — by him who has undertaken to be the covenant head of his people, and so to be their second Adam. I saw that before I actually sinned I had fallen by my first father’s sin; and I rejoiced that, for that very reason, it became possible in law for me to rise by a second head and representative. The fall by Adam left a loophole of escape; another Adam can undo the ruin made by the first. When I was anxious about whether a just God could possibly pardon me, I understood and saw by faith that he who is the Son of God became man, and in his own blessed person bore my sin in his own body on the tree. I saw that the punishment that brought me peace was laid on him, and that by his stripes I was healed. Dear friend, have you ever seen that? Have you ever understood how God can be just to the full, not canceling the penalty nor blunting the edge of the sword, and yet can be infinitely merciful, and can justify the ungodly who turn to him? It was because the Son of God, supremely glorious in his matchless person, undertook to vindicate the law by bearing the sentence due to me, that God is therefore able to pass by my sin. The law of God was more vindicated by the death of Christ than it would have been if all transgressors had been sent to hell. For the Son of God to suffer for sin upheld the government of God more gloriously than if the whole race had suffered.

Jesus has borne the death penalty on our behalf. See the wonder! There he hangs on the cross! This is the greatest sight you will ever see. Son of God and Son of Man, there he hangs, bearing unspeakable pains, the just for the unjust, to bring us to God. Oh, the glory of that sight! The innocent punished! The Holy One condemned! The Ever-blessed made a curse! The infinitely glorious put to a shameful death! The more I look at the sufferings of the Son of God, the surer I am that they must meet my case. Why did he suffer, if not to turn the penalty aside from us? If, then, he turned it aside by his death, it is turned aside, and those who believe in him need not fear it. It must be so: since expiation has been made, God is able to forgive without shaking the foundation of his throne, or blotting the statute book in the least degree. Conscience gets a full answer to her dreadful question. The wrath of God against iniquity, whatever that may be, must be terrible beyond all conception. Moses was right to say, “Who knows the power of Your anger?” Yet when we hear the Lord of glory cry, “Why have You forsaken Me?” and see him yielding up his spirit, we feel that the justice of God has been abundantly vindicated by obedience so perfect and death so terrible, rendered by so divine a person. If God himself bows before his own law, what more can be done? There is more in the atonement by way of merit than there is in all human sin by way of demerit. The great gulf of Jesus’ loving self-sacrifice can swallow up the mountains of our sins, all of them. For the sake of the infinite good of this one representative man, the Lord may well look with favor on other men, however unworthy they may be in and of themselves. It was a miracle of miracles that the Lord Jesus Christ should stand in our place, and

““Bear that we might never bear

His Father’s righteous ire.””

But he has done so. “It is finished.” God will spare the sinner because he did not spare his Son. God can pass by your transgressions because he laid those transgressions on his Only Begotten Son eighteen hundred years ago. If you believe in Jesus (that is the point), then your sins were carried away by him who was the scapegoat for his people.

What is it to believe in him? It is not merely to say, “He is God and the Savior,” but to trust him wholly and entirely, and take him for all your salvation from now on and forever — your Lord, your Master, your all. If you are willing to have Jesus, he has you already. If you believe in him, I tell you, you cannot go to hell; for that would make the sacrifice of Christ of no effect. It cannot be that a sacrifice should be accepted, and yet the soul for whom that sacrifice has been received should die. If the believing soul could be condemned, then why a sacrifice? If Jesus died in my place, why should I die also? Every believer can claim that the sacrifice was actually made for him: by faith he has laid his hands on it and made it his own, and therefore he may rest assured that he can never perish. The Lord would not receive this offering on our behalf and then condemn us to die. The Lord cannot read our pardon written in the blood of his own Son and then strike us down. That would be impossible. Oh, that you may be given grace at once to look away to Jesus and to begin at the beginning, that is, at Jesus, who is the fountainhead of mercy to guilty man!

“He justifies the ungodly.” “It is God who justifies,” and therefore, and for that reason only, it can be done, and he does it through the atoning sacrifice of his divine Son. So it can be justly done — so justly done that no one will ever question it — so thoroughly done that on the last dread day, when heaven and earth pass away, there will be no one to deny the validity of the justification. “Who is there to condemn? It is Christ who died. Who will bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies.”

Now, poor soul! Will you come into this lifeboat, just as you are? Here is safety from the wreck! Accept the sure deliverance. “I have nothing with me,” you say. You are not asked to bring anything with you. Men who escape for their lives will leave even their clothes behind. Leap for it, just as you are.

I will tell you this about myself to encourage you. My only hope of heaven lies in the full atonement made on Calvary’s cross for the ungodly. On that I firmly rely. I do not have the shadow of a hope anywhere else. You are in the same condition as I am; for neither of us has anything of our own worth thinking of as a ground of trust. Let us join hands and stand together at the foot of the cross, and trust our souls once for all to him who shed his blood for the guilty. We will be saved by one and the same Savior. If you perish trusting him, I must perish too. What more can I do to prove my own confidence in the gospel which I set before you?

Concerning Deliverance From Sinning

Here I want to say a plain word or two to those who understand the way of justification by faith which is in Christ Jesus, but whose trouble is that they cannot stop sinning. We can never be happy, at rest, or spiritually healthy until we become holy. We must be rid of sin; but how is that to be done? For many, this is the question of life or death. The old nature is very strong, and they have tried to curb and tame it; but it will not be subdued, and though they long to be better, they find themselves, if anything, growing worse than before. The heart is so hard, the will so stubborn, the passions so furious, the thoughts so fickle, the imagination so unruly, the desires so wild, that the man feels he has a den of wild beasts within him, which would sooner eat him up than be ruled by him. We may say of our fallen nature what the Lord said to Job about Leviathan: “Can you pet him like a bird or put him on a leash for your maidens?” A man might as well hope to hold the north wind in the hollow of his hand as expect to control, by his own strength, the raging powers that live within his fallen nature. This is a greater feat than any of the legendary labors of Hercules: God is needed here.

“I could believe that Jesus would forgive sin,” says one, “but then my trouble is that I sin again, and that I feel such terrible tendencies to evil within me. As surely as a stone thrown up into the air soon comes back down to the ground, so I, though earnest preaching sends me up to heaven, sink back again into my unfeeling state. Alas! I am easily bewitched by the basilisk eyes of sin, and so held as if under a spell that I cannot escape from my own folly.”

Dear friend, salvation would be a sadly incomplete thing if it did not deal with this part of our ruined state. We need to be purified as well as pardoned. Justification without sanctification would not be salvation at all. It would call the leper clean, and leave him to die of his disease; it would forgive the rebellion and allow the rebel to remain an enemy of his king. It would remove the consequences but overlook the cause, and that would leave us an endless and hopeless task. It would stop the stream for a time, but leave the fountain of defilement open, and sooner or later it would break out with greater power. Remember that the Lord Jesus came to take away sin in three ways: he came to remove the penalty of sin, the power of sin, and, at last, the presence of sin. You may reach the second at once — the power of sin may be broken immediately; and so you will be on the road to the third, that is, the removal of the presence of sin. “We know that He was manifested to take away our sins.”

The angel said of our Lord, “You are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins.” Our Lord Jesus came to destroy the works of the devil in us. What was said at our Lord’s birth was also declared at his death; for when the soldier pierced his side, blood and water came out at once, to picture the double cure by which we are set free from the guilt and the defilement of sin.

But if you are troubled about the power of sin and about the tendencies of your nature, as well you may be, here is a promise for you. Have faith in it, for it stands in the covenant of grace, which is ordered in all things and sure. God, who cannot lie, has said in Ezekiel 36:26:

““I will give you a new heart and I will put a new spirit within you; I will take away your heart of stone and I will give you a heart of flesh.””

You see, it is all “I will,” and “I will.” “I will give,” and “I will take away.” This is the royal language of the King of kings, who is able to do all that he wills. No word of his will ever fall to the ground.

The Lord knows very well that you cannot change your own heart and cannot cleanse your own nature; but he also knows that he can do both. He can make the Ethiopian change his skin, and the leopard its spots. Hear this, and be astonished: he can create you a second time; he can cause you to be born again. This is a miracle of grace, but the Holy Spirit will perform it. It would be a wonderful thing indeed if someone could stand at the foot of Niagara Falls and speak a word that would make the St. Lawrence River begin to run upstream, and leap up that great cliff over which it now pours with such immense force. Nothing but the power of God could achieve that marvel; yet it would be no more than a fitting parallel to what would happen if the course of your nature were completely reversed. All things are possible with God. He can reverse the direction of your desires and the current of your life, and instead of your going downward, away from God, he can make your whole being turn upward toward God. That is, in fact, what the Lord has promised to do for all who are in the covenant; and we know from Scripture that all believers are in the covenant. Let me read the words again:

““I will give you a new heart and I will put a new spirit within you; I will take away your heart of stone and I will give you a heart of flesh.””

What a wonderful promise! And it is yes and amen in Christ Jesus, to the glory of God through us. Let us take hold of it, accept it as true, and claim it for ourselves. Then it will be fulfilled in us, and in the days and years to come we will be singing of the wonderful change which the sovereign grace of God has worked in us.

It is well worth considering that when the Lord takes away the stony heart, that deed is done; and once it is done, no known power can ever take away the new heart he gives and the right spirit he puts within us. “God’s gifts and His call are without repentance”; that is, without repentance on his part; he does not take away what he has once given. Let him renew you, and you will be renewed. Man’s reforms and cleanings-up soon come to an end, for the dog returns to its vomit; but when God puts a new heart into us, the new heart is there forever, and it will never harden into stone again. He who made it flesh will keep it so. In this we may rejoice and be glad forever, in what God creates in the kingdom of his grace.

To put the matter very simply — have you ever heard Mr. Rowland Hill’s illustration of the cat and the sow? I will tell it in my own way, to illustrate our Savior’s vivid words — “You+ must be born again.” Do you see that cat? What a clean creature she is! How cleverly she washes herself with her tongue and her paws! It is quite a pretty sight! Have you ever seen a sow do that? No, you never have. It is against its nature. It would rather wallow in the mud. Go and teach a sow to wash itself, and see how little success you have. It would be a great improvement in hygiene if pigs would be clean. Teach them to wash and clean themselves as the cat has been doing! A useless task. You may wash that sow by force, but it hurries back to the mud and is soon as filthy as ever. The only way you can get a sow to wash itself is to turn it into a cat; then it will wash and be clean, but not until then! Suppose that change has been made, and then what was difficult or impossible is easy enough; from then on the pig will be fit for your living room and your hearth rug. So it is with an ungodly man. You cannot force him to do what a renewed man does most willingly; you may teach him and set him a good example, but he cannot learn the art of holiness, for he has no desire for it; his nature leads him another way. When the Lord makes a new man of him, then everything looks different. This change is so great that I once heard a convert say, “Either all the world is changed, or else I am.” The new nature goes after what is right as naturally as the old nature wanders after what is wrong. What a blessing to receive such a nature! Only the Holy Spirit can give it.

Has it ever struck you what a wonderful thing it is for the Lord to give a man a new heart and a right spirit? Perhaps you have seen a lobster that has fought with another lobster and lost one of its claws, and a new claw has grown. That is a remarkable thing; but it is far more astonishing that a man should be given a new heart. This, indeed, is a miracle beyond the powers of nature. Take a tree. If you cut off one of its branches, another may grow in its place; but can you change its nature? Can you sweeten sour sap? Can you make the thornbush bear figs? You can graft something better into it, and that is the parallel nature gives us to the work of grace; but to change the very life sap of the tree completely would be a miracle indeed. God works just such a marvel and mystery of power in all who believe in Jesus.

If you give yourself up to his divine working, the Lord will change your nature; he will subdue the old nature and breathe new life into you. Put your trust in the Lord Jesus Christ, and he will take the stony heart out of your flesh, and he will give you a heart of flesh. Where everything was hard, everything will be tender; where everything was wicked, everything will be virtuous; where everything tended downward, everything will rise upward with rushing force. The lion of anger will give way to the lamb of meekness; the raven of uncleanness will flee before the dove of purity; the vile serpent of deceit will be trampled under the heel of truth.

I have seen with my own eyes such marvelous changes in moral and spiritual character that I despair of no one. I could, if it were fitting, point out women who were once unchaste and are now as pure as the driven snow, and men who once blasphemed and now delight everyone around them by their intense devotion. Thieves are made honest, drunkards sober, liars truthful, and scoffers zealous. Wherever the grace of God has appeared to a man, it has trained him to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts, and to live a sober, righteous, and godly life in this present evil world; and, dear reader, it will do the same for you.

“I cannot make this change,” says one. Who said you could? The scripture we have quoted speaks not of what man will do, but of what God will do. It is God’s promise, and it is for him to fulfill his own pledges. Trust him to fulfill his word to you, and it will be done.

“But how is it to be done?” What business is that of yours? Must the Lord explain his methods before you will believe him? The Lord’s working in this matter is a great mystery: the Holy Spirit carries it out. The one who made the promise is responsible for keeping it, and he is equal to the task. God, who promises this marvelous change, will surely carry it out in all who receive Jesus, for to all of them he gives power to become the Sons of God. Oh, that you would believe it! Oh, that you would do the gracious Lord the justice of believing that he can and will do this for you, though it will be a great miracle! Oh, that you would believe that God cannot lie! Oh, that you would trust him for a new heart and a right spirit, for he can give them to you! May the Lord give you faith in his promise, faith in his Son, faith in the Holy Spirit, and faith in himself, and to him shall be praise and honor and glory forever and ever! Amen.

By Grace Through Faith

““By grace you+ have been saved through faith.” — Eph 2:8.”

I think it wise to step aside a little, so that I may ask my reader to look with adoration at the fountainhead of our salvation, which is the grace of God. “By grace you+ have been saved.” Because God is gracious, sinful men are forgiven, converted, purified, and saved. It is not because of anything in them, or anything that ever can be in them, that they are saved; but because of the boundless love, goodness, pity, compassion, mercy, and grace of God. Stop for a moment, then, at the wellspring. See the pure river of the water of life, as it flows out from the throne of God and of the Lamb!

What a bottomless deep the grace of God is! Who can measure its breadth? Who can fathom its depth? Like all the rest of the divine attributes, it is infinite. God is full of love, for “God is love.” God is full of goodness; the very name “God” is short for “good.” Boundless goodness and love are part of the very essence of the Godhead. It is because “His mercy endures forever” that men are not destroyed; because “His compassions never fail” that sinners are brought to him and forgiven.

Remember this well, or you+ may fall into error by fixing your+ minds so much on the faith which is the channel of salvation that you+ forget the grace which is the fountain and source even of faith itself. Faith is the work of God’s grace in us. No man can say that Jesus is the Christ except by the Holy Spirit. “No one can come to Me,” says Jesus, “unless the Father who sent Me draws him.” So faith, which is coming to Christ, is the result of God’s drawing. Grace is the first and last moving cause of salvation; and faith, essential as it is, is only an important part of the machinery which grace uses. We are saved “through faith,” but salvation is “by grace.” Sound out those words as if with the archangel’s trumpet: “By grace you+ have been saved.” What good news for the undeserving!

Faith holds the place of a channel or conduit. Grace is the fountain and the stream; faith is the aqueduct along which the flood of mercy flows down to refresh the thirsty sons of men. It is a great pity when the aqueduct is broken. It is a sad sight to see, around Rome, the many noble aqueducts which no longer carry water into the city, because the arches are broken and those marvelous structures are in ruins. The aqueduct must be kept whole to carry the flow; and in the same way faith must be true and sound, reaching right up to God and coming right down to us, so that it may become a useful channel of mercy to our souls.

Even so, I remind you again that faith is only the channel or aqueduct, and not the fountainhead, and we must not look at it so much that we exalt it above the divine source of all blessing, which lies in the grace of God. Never make a Christ out of your faith, and do not think of it as if it were the independent source of your salvation. Our life is found in “looking to Jesus,” not in looking to our own faith. By faith all things become possible to us; yet the power is not in the faith, but in the God on whom faith relies. Grace is the locomotive, and faith is the chain by which the carriage of the soul is coupled to the great driving power. The righteousness of faith is not the moral excellence of faith, but the righteousness of Jesus Christ, which faith grasps and makes its own. The peace within the soul does not come from looking at our own faith; it comes to us from him who is our peace: faith touches the hem of his garment, and power comes out of him into the soul.

See, then, dear friend, that the weakness of your faith will not destroy you. A trembling hand may receive a golden gift. The Lord’s salvation can come to us even if our faith is only like a grain of mustard seed. The power lies in the grace of God, and not in our faith. Great messages can be sent along slender wires, and the peace-giving witness of the Holy Spirit can reach the heart by means of a faith as thin as a thread, which seems hardly able to bear its own weight. Think more of him to whom you look than of the look itself. You must look away even from your own looking, and see nothing but Jesus, and the grace of God revealed in him.

Faith, What Is It?

What is this faith of which it is said, “By grace you+ have been saved, through faith”? There are many descriptions of faith; but almost all the definitions I have come across have made me understand it less than I did before I saw them. The negro said, when he read the chapter, that he would confound it; and very likely he did, though he meant to expound it. We may explain faith until nobody understands it. I hope I will not be guilty of that fault. Faith is the simplest of all things, and perhaps because of its simplicity it is all the harder to explain.

What is faith? It is made up of three things — Knowledge, belief, and trust. Knowledge comes first. “How can they believe in the One of whom they have not heard?” I need to be told a fact before I can possibly believe it. “Faith comes by hearing”; we must first hear, so that we may know what is to be believed. “Those who know Your name trust in You.” A measure of knowledge is essential to faith; that is why it is important to gain knowledge. “Incline your ear and come to Me; listen, so that your soul may live”: that was the word of the prophet of old, and it is still the word of the gospel. Search the Scriptures and learn what the Holy Spirit teaches about Christ and his salvation. Seek to know God: “For anyone who approaches Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him.” May the Holy Spirit give you the spirit of knowledge, and of the fear of the Lord! Know the gospel: know what the good news is, how it speaks of free forgiveness, and of a change of heart, of adoption into the family of God, and of countless other blessings. Know especially Christ Jesus the Son of God, the Savior of men, united to us by his human nature, and yet one with God, and so able to act as mediator between God and man, able to lay his hand on both, and to be the connecting link between the sinner and the Judge of all the earth. Strive to know more and more of Christ Jesus. Strive especially to know the doctrine of the sacrifice of Christ; for the point on which saving faith chiefly fixes itself is this — “God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not imputing men’s trespasses to them.” Know that Jesus was “made a curse for us, as it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree.’” Drink deeply of the doctrine of the substitutionary work of Christ; for in it lies the sweetest possible comfort for the guilty sons of men, since the Lord “made Him to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.” Faith begins with knowledge.

The mind goes on to believe that these things are true. The soul believes that God exists, and that he hears the cries of sincere hearts; that the gospel is from God; that justification by faith is the great truth which God has revealed in these last days by his Spirit more clearly than before. Then the heart believes that Jesus is really and truly our God and Savior, the Redeemer of men, the Prophet, Priest, and King of his people. All this is accepted as sure truth, not to be questioned. I pray that you may come to this at once. Come to believe firmly that “the blood of Jesus Christ, God’s dear Son, cleanses us from all sin”; that his sacrifice is complete and fully accepted by God on man’s behalf, so that he who believes in Jesus is not condemned. Believe these truths as you believe any other statements; for the difference between common faith and saving faith lies mainly in the things it is exercised on. Believe the witness of God just as you believe the testimony of your own father or friend. “If we accept the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater.”

So far you have advanced toward faith; only one more ingredient is needed to complete it, and that is trust. Commit yourself to the merciful God; rest your hope on the gracious gospel; entrust your soul to the dying and living Savior; wash away your sins in the atoning blood; accept his perfect righteousness, and all is well. Trust is the lifeblood of faith; there is no saving faith without it. The Puritans used to explain faith by the word “recumbency.” It means leaning on something. Lean with all your weight on Christ. It would be a better illustration still if I said: fall at full length, and lie on the Rock of Ages. Cast yourself on Jesus; rest in him; commit yourself to him. Once that is done, you have exercised saving faith. Faith is not a blind thing; for faith begins with knowledge. It is not a speculative thing; for faith believes facts of which it is sure. It is not an impractical, dreamy thing; for faith trusts, and stakes its destiny on the truth of revelation. That is one way of describing what faith is; I wonder whether I have “confounded” it already.

Let me try again. Faith is believing that Christ is what he is said to be, and that he will do what he has promised to do, and then expecting this of him. The Scriptures speak of Jesus Christ as being God, God in human flesh; as being perfect in his character; as being made a sin offering on our behalf; as bearing our sins in his own body on the tree. The Scripture speaks of him as having finished transgression, made an end of sin, and brought in everlasting righteousness. The sacred records also tell us that he “rose again from the dead,” that he “always lives to intercede for us,” that he has gone up into glory and taken possession of heaven on behalf of his people, and that he will soon come again “to judge the world with righteousness, and his people with equity.” We are to believe most firmly that this is so; for this is the testimony of God the Father, when he said, “This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!” God the Holy Spirit testifies to this as well; for the Spirit has borne witness to Christ, both in the inspired word and by various miracles, and by his working in the hearts of men. We are to believe that this testimony is true.

Faith also believes that Christ will do what he has promised; that since he has promised to cast out none who come to him, it is certain that he will not cast us out if we come to him. Faith believes that since Jesus said, “The water I give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life,” it must be true; and if we get this living water from Christ, it will remain in us, and will well up within us in streams of holy life. Whatever Christ has promised to do, he will do, and we must believe this, so that we look to his hands for pardon, justification, preservation, and eternal glory, just as he has promised them to those who believe in him.

Then comes the next necessary step. Jesus is what he is said to be; Jesus will do what he says he will do; therefore each one of us must trust him, saying, “He will be to me what he says he is, and he will do for me what he has promised to do; I leave myself in the hands of the one appointed to save, so that he may save me. I rest on his promise that he will do just as he has said.” This is a saving faith, and he who has it has everlasting life. Whatever his dangers and difficulties, whatever his darkness and depression, whatever his weaknesses and sins, he who believes in Christ Jesus in this way is not condemned, and will never come into condemnation.

May that explanation be of some use! I trust the Spirit of God may use it to lead my reader into peace at once. “Do not be afraid; only believe.” Trust, and be at rest.

My fear is that the reader may be content to understand what is to be done, and yet never do it. Better the poorest real faith actually at work than the finest ideal of it left in the realm of theory. The great thing is to believe in the Lord Jesus at once. Never mind distinctions and definitions. A hungry man eats though he does not understand the composition of his food, the anatomy of his mouth, or the process of digestion: he lives because he eats. Another, far cleverer man understands the science of nutrition thoroughly; but if he does not eat he will die, for all his knowledge. There are, no doubt, many in hell at this hour who understood the doctrine of faith, but did not believe. On the other hand, not one who has trusted in the Lord Jesus has ever been cast out, though he may never have been able to define his faith intelligently. O dear reader, receive the Lord Jesus into your soul, and you will live forever. “He who believes in Him has everlasting life.”

How May Faith Be Illustrated?

To make the matter of faith clearer still, I will give you a few illustrations. Though the Holy Spirit alone can make my reader see, it is my duty and my joy to give all the light I can, and to pray the divine Lord to open blind eyes. Oh, that my reader would pray the same prayer for himself!

The faith that saves has its parallels in the human body.

It is the eye that looks. By the eye we bring into the mind what is far away; we can bring the sun and the distant stars into the mind with a glance of the eye. So by trust we bring the Lord Jesus near to us; and though he is far away in heaven, he enters our heart. Only look to Jesus; for the hymn is strictly true—

““There is life in a look at the Crucified One,

There is life at this moment for thee.””

Faith is the hand that grasps. When our hand takes hold of anything for itself, it does exactly what faith does when it takes Christ and the blessings of his redemption as its own. Faith says, “Jesus is mine.” Faith hears of the pardoning blood, and cries, “I accept it to pardon me.” Faith calls the legacies of the dying Jesus her own; and they are her own, for faith is Christ’s heir; he has given himself and all that he has to faith. Take, my friend, what grace has provided for you. You will not be a thief, for you have divine permission: “Whoever desires, let him take the water of life freely.” The man who may have a treasure simply by grasping it will be foolish indeed if he remains poor.

Faith is the mouth that feeds on Christ. Before food can nourish us, it must be taken into us. This is a simple matter — this eating and drinking. We willingly take our food into the mouth, and then we consent to its passing down into our inner parts, where it is taken up and absorbed into our body. Paul says, in his Epistle to the Romans, in the tenth chapter, “The word is near you; it is in your mouth.” Now then, all that remains to be done is to swallow it, to let it go down into the soul. Oh, that men had an appetite! For the man who is hungry and sees food before him does not need to be taught how to eat. “Give me,” said one, “a knife and a fork and a chance.” He was quite ready to do the rest. Truly, a heart that hungers and thirsts after Christ has only to know that he is freely given, and it will receive him at once. If my reader is in that state, let him receive Jesus without hesitating; for he may be sure that he will never be blamed for doing so: “for to all who did receive Him, He gave the right to become sons of God.” He never turns anyone away, but he gives all who come the right to remain sons forever.

The occupations of daily life illustrate faith in many ways. The farmer buries good seed in the earth, and expects it not only to live but to be multiplied. He has faith in God’s covenant that seedtime and harvest shall not cease, and he is rewarded for his faith.

The merchant places his money in the care of a banker, and trusts entirely to the honesty and soundness of the bank. He entrusts his capital to another’s hands, and feels far more at ease than if he had the solid gold locked up in an iron safe.

The sailor trusts himself to the sea. When he swims he takes his foot off the bottom and rests on the buoyant ocean. He could not swim if he did not throw himself wholly on the water.

The goldsmith puts precious metal into the fire, which seems eager to consume it, but he gets it back from the furnace purified by the heat.

You cannot turn anywhere in life without seeing faith at work between man and man, or between man and the laws of nature. Now, just as we trust in daily life, so we are to trust in God as he reveals himself in Christ Jesus.

Faith exists in different people in different degrees, according to the amount of their knowledge or their growth in grace. Sometimes faith is little more than a simple clinging to Christ: a sense of dependence and a willingness to depend in that way. When you are down at the seaside you will see limpets sticking to the rock. You walk softly up to the rock; you strike the limpet a quick blow with your walking stick, and off he comes. Try the next limpet the same way. You have given him warning; he heard the blow with which you struck his neighbor, and he clings with all his might. You will never get him off — not you! Strike, and strike again, but you will break the rock first. Our little friend, the limpet, does not know much, but he clings. He knows nothing of the geology of the rock, but he clings. He can cling, and he has found something to cling to: this is his whole stock of knowledge, and he uses it for his security and salvation. It is the limpet’s life to cling to the rock, and it is the sinner’s life to cling to Jesus. Thousands of God’s people have no more faith than this; they know enough to cling to Jesus with all their heart and soul, and this is enough for present peace and eternal safety. Jesus Christ is to them a Savior strong and mighty, a rock that cannot be moved or changed; they hold on to him for dear life, and this clinging saves them. Reader, can you not cling? Do so at once.

Faith is seen when one man relies on another because he knows the other is greater than himself. This is a higher faith: the faith that knows the reason for its dependence, and acts on it. I do not think the limpet knows much about the rock; but as faith grows it becomes more and more intelligent. A blind man trusts himself to his guide because he knows that his friend can see, and, trusting, he walks where his guide leads him. If the poor man was born blind he does not know what sight is; but he knows that there is such a thing as sight, and that his friend has it, and so he freely puts his hand into the hand of the one who sees, and follows his lead. “We walk by faith, not by sight.” “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.” This is as good a picture of faith as there could be; we know that Jesus has merit, and power, and blessing, which we do not have, and so we gladly trust ourselves to him, to be to us what we cannot be to ourselves. We trust him as the blind man trusts his guide. He never betrays our confidence; but he “has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, sanctification, and redemption.”

Every boy who goes to school has to exercise faith while he learns. His teacher teaches him geography, and tells him about the shape of the earth and the existence of certain great cities and empires. The boy does not himself know that these things are true, except that he believes his teacher and the books put into his hands. That is what you will have to do with Christ, if you are to be saved: you must simply know because he tells you, believe because he assures you it is so, and trust yourself to him because he promises you that salvation will be the result. Almost all that you and I know has come to us by faith. A scientific discovery has been made, and we are sure of it. On what grounds do we believe it? On the authority of certain well-known men of learning, whose reputations are established. We have never made or seen their experiments, but we believe their testimony. You must do the same with Jesus: because he teaches you certain truths, you are to be his disciple and believe his words; because he has performed certain acts, you are to be his client and trust yourself to him. He is infinitely greater than you, and offers himself to your trust as your Master and Lord. If you will receive him and his words, you will be saved.

Another and higher form of faith is the faith that grows out of love. Why does a boy trust his father? The reason the child trusts his father is that he loves him. Blessed and happy are those who have a sweet faith in Jesus, intertwined with deep affection for him, for this is a restful confidence. These lovers of Jesus are charmed by his character and delighted with his mission; they are carried away by the loving-kindness that he has shown, and so they cannot help trusting him, because they admire, revere, and love him so much.

Loving trust in the Savior may be illustrated like this. A lady is the wife of the most eminent physician of the day. She is taken with a dangerous illness, and is struck down by its power; yet she is wonderfully calm and quiet, for her husband has made this disease his special study, and has healed thousands who suffered from it. She is not in the least troubled, for she feels perfectly safe in the hands of one so dear to her, in whom skill and love are blended in their highest forms. Her faith is reasonable and natural; her husband, from every point of view, deserves it from her. This is the kind of faith which the happiest of believers place in Christ. There is no physician like him; none can save as he can. We love him, and he loves us, and so we put ourselves into his hands, accept whatever he prescribes, and do whatever he tells us. We feel that nothing can be wrongly arranged while he is directing our affairs; for he loves us too well to let us perish, or suffer a single needless pang.

Faith is the root of obedience, and this may be clearly seen in everyday life. When a captain trusts a pilot to steer his ship into port, he handles the ship as the pilot directs. When a traveler trusts a guide to lead him over a difficult pass, he follows the path his guide points out. When a patient believes in a physician, he carefully follows his prescriptions and directions. Faith that refuses to obey the commands of the Savior is a mere pretense, and will never save the soul. We trust Jesus to save us; he gives us directions about the way of salvation; we follow those directions and are saved. Let my reader not forget this. Trust Jesus, and prove your trust by doing whatever he tells you.

A notable form of faith arises from sure knowledge; this comes from growth in grace, and is the faith that believes Christ because it knows him, and trusts him because it has tested him and found him unfailingly faithful. An old Christian used to write T and P in the margin of her Bible whenever she had tried and proved a promise. How easy it is to trust a tried and proved Savior! You cannot do this yet, but you will. Everything must have a beginning. You will rise to strong faith in due time. This mature faith does not ask for signs and tokens, but bravely believes. Look at the faith of the master mariner — I have often marveled at it. He casts off his cable; he steams away from the land. For days, weeks, or even months, he sees neither sail nor shore; yet on he goes, day and night, without fear, until one morning he finds himself exactly opposite the desired haven he has been steering for. How has he found his way across the trackless deep? He has trusted in his compass, his nautical almanac, his glass, and the heavenly bodies; and by following their guidance, without sighting land, he has steered so accurately that he does not have to change course by a single point to enter port. It is a wonderful thing — that sailing or steaming without sight. Spiritually it is a blessed thing to leave the shores of sight and feeling altogether, and to say “Goodbye” to inward feelings, cheering providences, signs, tokens, and so on. It is glorious to be far out on the ocean of divine love, believing in God, and steering straight for heaven by the directions of the Word of God. “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed”; an abundant entrance will be administered to them at the last, and a safe voyage on the way. Will my reader not put his trust in God in Christ Jesus? There I rest with joyful confidence. Brother, come with me, and believe our Father and our Savior. Come at once.

Why Are We Saved By Faith?

Why is Faith chosen as the channel of Salvation? No doubt this question is often asked. “By grace you+ have been saved through faith,” is certainly the doctrine of Holy Scripture and the ordinance of God; but why is it so? Why is faith chosen rather than hope, or love, or patience?

It befits us to be modest in answering such a question, for God’s ways are not always to be understood; nor are we allowed to question them presumptuously. We would humbly reply that, as far as we can tell, faith has been chosen as the channel of grace because there is a natural fitness in faith to be used as the receiver. Suppose I am about to give a poor man a gift: I put it into his hand — why? Well, it would hardly be fitting to put it into his ear, or to lay it on his foot; the hand seems made on purpose to receive. So, in the makeup of our minds, faith is created for the very purpose of being a receiver: it is the man’s hand, and there is a fitness in receiving grace by means of it.

Let me put this very plainly. Faith that receives Christ is as simple an act as when your child takes an apple from you, because you hold it out and promise to give him the apple if he comes for it. The believing and the receiving concern only an apple; but they make up exactly the same act as the faith that deals with eternal salvation. What the child’s hand is to the apple, your faith is to the perfect salvation of Christ. The child’s hand does not make the apple, nor improve the apple, nor deserve the apple; it only takes it; and faith is chosen by God to be the receiver of salvation, because it does not claim to create salvation, nor to help in it, but is content to receive it humbly. “Faith is the tongue that begs pardon, the hand which receives it, and the eye which sees it; but it is not the price which buys it.” Faith never makes herself her own plea; she rests her whole case on the blood of Christ. She makes a good servant for bringing the riches of the Lord Jesus to the soul, because she acknowledges where she got them, and confesses that grace alone entrusted her with them.

Again, faith is no doubt chosen because it gives all the glory to God.
