It is by faith so that it may be by grace, and it is by grace so that there may be no boasting; for God cannot bear pride. “The proud He knows from afar,” and he has no wish to come nearer to them. He will not give salvation in a way that would suggest or foster pride. Paul says, “Not by works, so that no one can boast.” Now, faith shuts out all boasting. The hand that receives charity does not say, “I should be thanked for accepting the gift”; that would be absurd. When the hand carries bread to the mouth, it does not say to the body, “Thank me; for I feed you.” What the hand does is a very simple thing, though a very necessary one; and it never claims glory for itself for what it does. So God has chosen faith to receive the unspeakable gift of his grace, because it cannot take any credit to itself, but must adore the gracious God who is the giver of all good. Faith sets the crown on the right head, and therefore the Lord Jesus used to put the crown on the head of faith, saying, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

Next, God chooses faith as the channel of salvation because it is a sure means of linking man with God. When man trusts in God, there is a point of union between them, and that union guarantees blessing. Faith saves us because it makes us cling to God, and so brings us into connection with him. I have often used the following illustration, but I must repeat it, because I cannot think of a better one. I am told that years ago a boat capsized above Niagara Falls, and two men were being carried down by the current, when people on the shore managed to float a rope out to them, and both of them seized it. One of them held on tight and was pulled safely to the bank; but the other, seeing a great log come floating by, unwisely let go of the rope and clung to the log, for it was the bigger of the two things, and seemed better to cling to. Alas! The log, with the man on it, went right over into the vast abyss, because there was no union between the log and the shore. The size of the log was no help to the man who grasped it; it needed a connection with the shore to bring him to safety. So when a man trusts in his works, or in sacraments, or in anything of that kind, he will not be saved, because there is no link between him and Christ; but faith, though it may seem like a slender cord, is in the hand of the great God on the shore; infinite power pulls in the connecting line, and so draws the man out of destruction. Oh, the blessedness of faith, for it unites us to God!

Again, faith is chosen because it touches the mainsprings of action. Even in ordinary things, faith of a sort lies at the root of everything. I wonder whether I would be wrong to say that we never do anything except through faith of some kind. If I walk across my study, it is because I believe my legs will carry me. A man eats because he believes in the necessity of food; he goes to work because he believes in the value of money; he accepts a check because he believes that the bank will honor it. Columbus discovered America because he believed that there was another continent beyond the ocean; and the Pilgrim Fathers colonized it because they believed that God would be with them on those rocky shores. Most great deeds have been born of faith; for good or for evil, faith works wonders through the man in whom it lives. Faith in its natural form is an all-prevailing force, which enters into every kind of human action. Perhaps the man who mocks faith in God is the very one who, in an evil form, has the most faith of all; indeed, he usually falls into a gullibility that would be ridiculous if it were not disgraceful. God gives salvation to faith because, by creating faith in us, he touches the real mainspring of our emotions and actions. He has, so to speak, taken possession of the battery, and now he can send the sacred current to every part of our nature. When we believe in Christ, and the heart has come into God’s possession, then we are saved from sin, and are moved toward repentance, holiness, zeal, prayer, consecration, and every other gracious thing. “What oil is to the wheels, what weights are to a clock, what wings are to a bird, what sails are to a ship, that faith is to all holy duties and services.” Have faith, and all the other graces will follow and keep on their course.

Again, faith has the power of working by love; it moves the affections toward God, and draws the heart after the best things. He who believes in God will, beyond all question, love God. Faith is an act of the understanding; but it also comes from the heart. “With the heart man believes and is justified”; and so God gives salvation to faith because it lives next door to the affections and is closely related to love; and love is the parent and the nurse of every holy feeling and act. Love for God is obedience; love for God is holiness. To love God and to love man is to be conformed to the image of Christ; and this is salvation.

Moreover, faith creates peace and joy; he who has it rests, and is calm, is glad and joyful; and this is a preparation for heaven. God gives all heavenly gifts to faith, for this reason among others: that faith produces in us the life and spirit which are to be shown forever in the higher and better world. Faith supplies us with armor for this life, and education for the life to come. It enables a man both to live and to die without fear; it prepares him both for action and for suffering; and so the Lord chooses it as a most fitting means of bringing grace to us, and in this way securing us for glory.

Certainly faith does for us what nothing else can do; it gives us joy and peace, and brings us into rest. Why do men try to gain salvation by other means? An old theologian says, “A foolish servant who is told to open a door sets his shoulder to it and pushes with all his might; but the door does not stir, and he cannot enter, whatever strength he uses. Another comes with a key, and easily unlocks the door, and enters very readily. Those who would be saved by works are pushing at heaven’s gate without result; but faith is the key which opens the gate at once.” Reader, will you not use that key? The Lord commands you to believe in his dear Son, so you may do so; and if you do, you will live. Is this not the promise of the gospel, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved”? Mark 16:16. What objection can you have to a way of salvation that commends itself to the mercy and the wisdom of our gracious God?

Alas! I Can Do Nothing!

After the anxious heart has accepted the doctrine of atonement and learned the great truth that salvation is by faith in the Lord Jesus, it is often sorely troubled by a sense of being unable to do anything good. Many are groaning, “I can do nothing.” They are not making this an excuse; they feel it as a daily burden. They would if they could. Each one of them can honestly say, “To will is present with me, but how to do what I would, I do not find.”

This feeling seems to make the whole gospel null and void; for what use is food to a hungry man if he cannot get at it? What good is the river of the water of life if one cannot drink? We all remember the story of the doctor and the poor woman’s child. The learned doctor told the mother that her little one would soon be better with proper treatment, but it was absolutely necessary that her boy should regularly drink the best port wine, and that he should spend some time at one of the German spas. This, to a widow who could hardly get bread to eat! Now, it sometimes seems to the troubled heart that the simple gospel of “Believe and live” is not, after all, so very simple; for it asks the poor sinner to do what he cannot do. To those who are truly awakened but only half taught, there seems to be a missing link: over there is the salvation of Jesus, but how is it to be reached? The soul is without strength and does not know what to do. It lies within sight of the city of refuge and cannot enter its gate.

Is this lack of strength provided for in the plan of salvation? It is. The work of the Lord is perfect. It begins where we are, and asks nothing of us to complete it. When the good Samaritan saw the traveler lying wounded and half dead, he did not tell him to get up and come to him, and climb on the donkey and ride off to the inn. No, “he came where he was,” and cared for him, and lifted him onto the animal and carried him to the inn. This is how the Lord Jesus deals with us in our low and wretched state.

We have seen that God justifies, that he justifies the ungodly, and that he justifies them through faith in the precious blood of Jesus; now we have to see the condition these ungodly ones are in when Jesus works out their salvation. Many awakened people are troubled not only about their sin but about their moral weakness. They have no strength to escape from the mire into which they have fallen, nor to keep out of it in the days to come. They grieve not only over what they have done, but over what they cannot do. They feel powerless, helpless, and spiritually lifeless. It may sound odd to say that they feel dead, and yet that is how it is. In their own eyes they are incapable of any good. They cannot travel the road to heaven, for their bones are broken. “None of the men of strength could lift a hand”; in fact, they are “without strength.” Happily, it is written, as the demonstration of God’s great love to us:

““When we were still without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” — Rom 5:6.”

Here we see conscious helplessness rescued — rescued by the intervention of the Lord Jesus. Our helplessness is extreme. It is not written, “When we were comparatively weak Christ died for us”; or, “When we had only a little strength”; but the description is absolute and unrestricted: “When we were still without strength.” We had no strength at all that could help in our salvation; our Lord’s words were emphatically true, “Apart from Me you+ can do nothing.” I may go further than the text, and remind you of the great love with which the Lord loved us, “even when we were dead in our trespasses and sins.” To be dead is even more than to be without strength.

The one thing that the poor sinner who has no strength must fix his mind on, and hold firmly, as his one ground of hope, is the divine assurance that “in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” Believe this, and all inability will disappear. As the fable says of Midas that he turned everything into gold by his touch, so it is true of faith that it turns everything it touches into good. Our very needs and weaknesses become blessings when faith deals with them.

Let us look at some of the forms this lack of strength takes. To begin with, one man will say, “Sir, I do not seem to have the strength to gather my thoughts and keep them fixed on the solemn matters that concern my salvation: a short prayer is almost too much for me. This is partly, perhaps, from natural weakness, partly because I have harmed myself by dissipation, and partly also because I worry myself with worldly cares, so that I am not capable of the high thoughts that are necessary before a soul can be saved.” This is a very common form of sinful weakness. Listen to me! You are without strength on this point, and there are many like you. They could not follow a train of connected thought to save their lives. Many poor men and women are illiterate and untrained, and they would find deep thinking very heavy work. Others are so light and frivolous by nature that they could no more follow a long line of argument and reasoning than they could fly. They could never reach the knowledge of any deep mystery if they spent their whole life trying. You need not, therefore, despair: what is necessary to salvation is not sustained thought, but a simple reliance on Jesus. Hold on to this one fact — “In due time Christ died for the ungodly.” This truth will not require from you any deep research or profound reasoning or convincing argument. There it stands: “In due time Christ died for the ungodly.” Fix your mind on that, and rest there.

Let this one great, gracious, glorious fact lie in your spirit till it perfumes all your thoughts, and makes you rejoice even though you are without strength, since the Lord Jesus has become your strength and your song; yes, he has become your salvation. It is a fact revealed in the Scriptures that in due time Christ died for the ungodly when they were still without strength. You have heard these words hundreds of times, perhaps, and yet you have never before seen their meaning. There is a cheering flavor about them, is there not? Jesus did not die for our righteousness; he died for our sins. He did not come to save us because we were worth saving, but because we were utterly worthless, ruined, and lost. He did not come to earth for any reason found in us, but solely and only for reasons he drew from the depths of his own divine love. In due time he died for those whom he describes, not as godly, but as ungodly, applying to them as hopeless an adjective as he could well have chosen. If your understanding is small, still fasten it to this truth, which fits the smallest capacity and is able to cheer the heaviest heart. Let this text lie under your tongue like a sweet morsel, till it dissolves into your heart and flavors all your thoughts; and then it will matter little if those thoughts are as scattered as autumn leaves. People who have never shone in science, nor shown the least originality of mind, have still been fully able to accept the doctrine of the cross, and have been saved by it. Why should you not?

I hear another man cry, “Oh, sir, my lack of strength lies mainly in this, that I cannot repent enough.” What a curious idea men have of what repentance is! Many imagine that so many tears must be shed, and so many groans heaved, and so much despair endured. Where does this unreasonable notion come from? Unbelief and despair are sins, and so I do not see how they can be parts of an acceptable repentance; yet there are many who regard them as necessary parts of true Christian experience. They are greatly mistaken. Still, I know what they mean, for in the days of my darkness I used to feel the same way. I wanted to repent, but I thought that I could not do it, and yet all the while I was repenting. Odd as it may sound, I felt that I could not feel. I used to get into a corner and weep because I could not weep; and I fell into bitter sorrow because I could not sorrow for sin. What a jumble it all is when, in our unbelieving state, we begin to judge our own condition! It is like a blind man looking at his own eyes. My heart melted within me for fear, because I thought that my heart was as hard as flint. My heart was broken to think that it would not break. Now I can see that I was showing the very thing that I thought I did not have; but then I did not know where I was.

Oh, that I could help others into the light I now enjoy. How gladly I would say a word that might shorten the time of their confusion. I would say a few plain words, and pray “the Comforter” to apply them to the heart.

Remember that the man who truly repents is never satisfied with his own repentance. We can no more repent perfectly than we can live perfectly. However pure our tears, there will always be some dirt in them: there will be something to repent of even in our best repentance. But listen! To repent is to change your mind about sin, and Christ, and all the great things of God. Sorrow is implied in this; but the main point is the turning of the heart from sin to Christ. If there is this turning, you have the essence of true repentance, even though no alarm and no despair have ever cast their shadow on your mind.

If you cannot repent as you would like, it will greatly help you to do so if you will firmly believe that “in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” Think of this again and again. How can you go on being hard-hearted when you know that out of supreme love “Christ died for the ungodly”? Let me persuade you to reason with yourself like this: Ungodly as I am, though this heart of steel will not relent, though I beat my breast in vain, yet he died for such as I am, since he died for the ungodly. Oh, that I may believe this and feel its power on my flinty heart!

Blot out every other thought from your soul, and sit down for hours at a time, and meditate deeply on this one splendid display of unmerited, unexpected, unequaled love, “Christ died for the ungodly.” Read carefully the account of the Lord’s death as you find it in the four Gospels. If anything can melt your stubborn heart, it will be a sight of the sufferings of Jesus, and the thought that he suffered all this for his enemies.

““O Jesus! sweet the tears I shed,

While at thy feet I kneel,

Gaze on thy wounded, fainting head,

And all thy sorrows feel.”

““My heart dissolves to see thee bleed,

This heart so hard before;

I hear thee for the guilty plead,

And grief o’erflows the more.”

““’Twas for the sinful thou didst die,

And I a sinner stand:

Convinc’d by thine expiring eye,

Slain by thy pierced hand.””

Surely the cross is that wonder-working rod that can bring water out of a rock. If you understand the full meaning of the divine sacrifice of Jesus, you must repent of ever having opposed one who is so full of love. It is written, “They will look on Me, the One they have pierced. They will mourn for Him as one mourns for an only child, and grieve bitterly for Him as one grieves for a firstborn son.” Repentance will not make you see Christ; but seeing Christ will give you repentance. You must not make a Christ out of your repentance, but you must look to Christ for repentance. The Holy Spirit, by turning us to Christ, turns us from sin. Look away, then, from the effect to the cause, from your own repenting to the Lord Jesus, who is exalted on high to give repentance.

I have heard another say, “I am tormented with horrible thoughts. Wherever I go, blasphemies creep in on me. Often at my work a dreadful suggestion forces itself on me, and even in my bed I am startled out of my sleep by whispers of the evil one. I cannot get away from this horrible temptation.” Friend, I know what you mean, for I myself have been hunted by this wolf. A man might as well hope to fight a swarm of flies with a sword as to master his own thoughts when the devil sets them on him. A poor tempted soul, attacked by Satan’s suggestions, is like a traveler I have read of, about whose head and ears and whole body there came a swarm of angry bees. He could not keep them off or escape from them. They stung him everywhere and threatened to be the death of him. I do not wonder you feel that you are without strength to stop these hideous and abominable thoughts which Satan pours into your soul; but still I would remind you of the Scripture before us — “When we were still without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” Jesus knew where we were and where we would be; he saw that we could not overcome the prince of the power of the air; he knew that we would be greatly harassed by him; but even then, when he saw us in that condition, Christ died for the ungodly. Cast the anchor of your faith on this. The devil himself cannot tell you that you are not ungodly; believe, then, that Jesus died even for such as you are. Remember Martin Luther’s way of cutting off the devil’s head with his own sword. “Oh,” said the devil to Martin Luther, “you are a sinner.” “Yes,” he said, “Christ died to save sinners.” So he struck him with his own sword. Hide in this refuge, and stay there: “In due time Christ died for the ungodly.” If you stand by that truth, your blasphemous thoughts, which you have not the strength to drive away, will go away of themselves; for Satan will see that he gains nothing by plaguing you with them.

These thoughts, if you hate them, are not yours at all, but are things thrust in by the devil, and he is responsible for them, not you. If you fight against them, they are no more yours than are the curses and lies of rioters in the street. It is by means of these thoughts that the devil would drive you to despair, or at least keep you from trusting Jesus. The poor diseased woman could not come to Jesus because of the crowd, and you are in much the same condition, because of the rush and throng of these dreadful thoughts. Still, she put out her finger and touched the fringe of the Lord’s garment, and she was healed. Do the same.

Jesus died for those who are guilty of “every sin and blasphemy”; and so I am sure he will not refuse those who are unwilling captives of evil thoughts. Cast yourself on him, thoughts and all, and see if he is not mighty to save. He can silence those horrible whisperings of the fiend, or he can enable you to see them in their true light, so that you are not troubled by them. In his own way he can and will save you, and in the end give you perfect peace. Only trust him for this and everything else.

That form of inability which lies in a supposed lack of power to believe is sadly perplexing. We are not strangers to the cry —

““Oh that I could believe,

Then all would easy be;

I would, but cannot; Lord, relieve,

My help must come from thee.””

Many remain in the dark for years because they have no power, as they say, to do what is in fact the giving up of all power and resting in the power of another, the Lord Jesus. Indeed, this whole matter of believing is a very curious thing; for people do not get much help by trying to believe. Believing does not come by trying. If someone told me of something that happened today, I would not tell him that I would try to believe him. If I trusted the truthfulness of the man who told me the incident and said that he saw it, I would accept what he said at once. If I did not think him an honest man, I would, of course, disbelieve him; but there would be no trying in the matter. Now, when God declares that there is salvation in Christ Jesus, I must either believe him at once or make him a liar. Surely you will not hesitate over which is the right path here. The witness of God must be true, and we are bound to believe in Jesus at once.

But perhaps you have been trying to believe too much. Now, do not aim at great things. Be satisfied to have a faith that can hold in its hand this one truth, “While we were still without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” He laid down his life for men while they were not yet believing in him, nor able to believe in him. He died for men, not as believers, but as sinners. He came to make these sinners into believers and saints; but when he died for them he saw them as utterly without strength. If you hold to the truth that Christ died for the ungodly, and believe it, your faith will save you, and you may go in peace. If you will trust your soul to Jesus, who died for the ungodly, then even though you cannot believe all things, nor move mountains, nor do any other wonderful works, you are saved. It is not great faith but true faith that saves; and the salvation lies not in the faith, but in the Christ in whom faith trusts. Faith like a grain of mustard seed will bring salvation. It is not the measure of faith, but the sincerity of faith, that matters. Surely a man can believe what he knows to be true; and as you know Jesus to be true, you, my friend, can believe in him.

The cross, which is the object of faith, is also, by the power of the Holy Spirit, its cause. Sit down and watch the dying Savior till faith springs up spontaneously in your heart. There is no place like Calvary for creating confidence. The air of that sacred hill brings health to trembling faith. Many who have watched there have said:

““While I view thee, wounded, grieving,

Breathless on the cursed tree,

Lord, I feel my heart believing

That thou suffer’dst thus for me.””

“Alas!” cries another, “my lack of strength lies here: I cannot quit my sin, and I know that I cannot go to heaven and take my sin with me.” I am glad you know that, for it is quite true. You must be divorced from your sin, or you cannot be married to Christ. Remember the question that flashed into the mind of young Bunyan when he was at his games on the green on Sunday: “Will you have your sins and go to hell, or will you quit your sins and go to heaven?” That stopped him dead. That is a question every man will have to answer; for there is no going on in sin and going to heaven. That cannot be. You must quit sin or quit hope. Do you reply, “Yes, I am willing enough. To will is present with me, but how to do what I would, I do not find. Sin masters me, and I have no strength”? Come, then, if you have no strength, this text is still true, “When we were still without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” Can you still believe that? However other things may seem to contradict it, will you believe it? God has said it, and it is a fact; so hold on to it for dear life, for your only hope lies there. Believe this and trust Jesus, and you will soon find power to slay your sin; but apart from him, the strong man, fully armed, will hold you as his bond-slave forever. For my part, I could never have overcome my own sinfulness. I tried and failed. My evil tendencies were too many for me, till, believing that Christ died for me, I cast my guilty soul on him, and then I received a conquering principle by which I overcame my sinful self. The doctrine of the cross can be used to slay sin, just as the old warriors used their huge two-handed swords and mowed down their foes at every stroke. There is nothing like faith in the Sinner’s Friend: it overcomes all evil. If Christ has died for me, ungodly as I am, without strength as I am, then I cannot live in sin any longer, but must rouse myself to love and serve him who has redeemed me. I cannot trifle with the evil that killed my best friend. I must be holy for his sake. How can I live in sin when he has died to save me from it?

See what a splendid help it is to you who are without strength to know and believe that in due time Christ died for such ungodly ones as you are. Have you caught the idea yet? Somehow it is so difficult for our darkened, prejudiced, and unbelieving minds to see the essence of the gospel. At times, when I have finished preaching, I have thought that I set out the gospel so clearly that the nose on one’s face could not be plainer; and yet I find that even intelligent hearers have failed to understand what was meant by “Look to Me, and be saved.” Converts usually say that they did not know the gospel till such and such a day; and yet they had heard it for years. The gospel is unknown, not from lack of explanation, but from the absence of personal revelation. This the Holy Spirit is ready to give, and will give to those who ask him. Yet when it is given, the whole of the truth revealed lies within these words: “Christ died for the ungodly.”

I hear another lamenting like this: “Oh, sir, my weakness lies in this, that I do not seem to stay of one mind for long. I hear the word on a Sunday, and I am moved; but during the week I meet an evil companion, and my good feelings are all gone. The men I work with do not believe in anything, and they say such terrible things, and I do not know how to answer them, and so I find myself knocked over.” I know this Plastic Pliable very well, and I tremble for him; but at the same time, if he is really sincere, his weakness can be met by divine grace. The Holy Spirit can cast out the evil spirit of the fear of man. He can make the coward brave. Remember, my poor wavering friend, you must not remain in this state. It will never do to be mean and beggarly to yourself. Stand up straight, and look at yourself, and see if you were ever meant to be like a toad under a harrow, afraid for your life either to move or to stand still. Do have a mind of your own. This is not only a spiritual matter, but one that concerns ordinary manliness. I would do many things to please my friends; but to go to hell to please them is more than I would risk. It may be all very well to do this and that for the sake of good company; but it will never do to lose the friendship of God in order to stay on good terms with men. “I know that,” says the man, “but still, though I know it, I cannot pluck up courage. I cannot show my colors. I cannot stand firm.” Well, to you also I bring the same text: “When we were still without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.” If Peter were here, he would say, “The Lord Jesus died for me even when I was such a poor weak creature that the servant girl who kept the fire drove me to lie, and to swear that I did not know the Lord.” Yes, Jesus died for those who deserted him and fled. Take a firm grip of this truth — “Christ died for the ungodly while they were still without strength.” This is your way out of your cowardice. Get this worked into your soul, “Christ died for me,” and you will soon be ready to die for him. Believe that he suffered in your place and stead, and offered for you a full, true, and satisfactory expiation. If you believe that fact, you will be compelled to feel, “I cannot be ashamed of him who died for me.” A full conviction that this is true will steel you with fearless courage. Look at the saints in the age of the martyrs. In the early days of Christianity, when this great thought of Christ’s surpassing love was sparkling in all its freshness in the church, men were not only ready to die, but grew eager to suffer, and even presented themselves by the hundreds at the rulers’ judgment seats, confessing Christ. I do not say that they were wise to seek a cruel death; but it proves my point, that a sense of the love of Jesus lifts the mind above all fear of what man can do to us. Why should it not have the same effect in you? Oh, that it might now inspire you with a brave resolve to come out on the Lord’s side, and be his follower to the end!

May the Holy Spirit help us to come this far by faith in the Lord Jesus, and all will be well!

The Increase Of Faith

How can we gain an increase of faith? This is a very earnest question to many. They say they want to believe, but cannot. A great deal of nonsense is talked on this subject. Let us be strictly practical in dealing with it. Common sense is as much needed in religion as anywhere else. “What am I to do in order to believe?” Someone who was asked the best way to do a certain simple thing replied that the best way to do it was to do it at once. We waste time discussing methods when the action is simple. The shortest way to believe is to believe. If the Holy Spirit has made you open-minded, you will believe as soon as the truth is set before you. You will believe it because it is true. The gospel command is clear: “Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved.” It is idle to dodge this with questions and quibbles. The order is plain; let it be obeyed.

But still, if you have a difficulty, take it to God in prayer. Tell the great Father exactly what it is that puzzles you, and beg him by his Holy Spirit to solve the question. If I cannot believe a statement in a book, I am glad to ask the author what he means by it; and if he is an honest man, his explanation will satisfy me: how much more will the divine explanation of the hard points of Scripture satisfy the heart of the true seeker. The Lord is willing to make himself known; go to him and see if it is not so. Go at once to your inner room, and cry, “O Holy Spirit, lead me into the truth. What I do not know, teach me.”

Furthermore, if faith seems difficult, it may be that God the Holy Spirit will enable you to believe if you hear very often and earnestly what you are commanded to believe. We believe many things because we have heard them so often. Do you not find it so in everyday life, that if you hear a thing fifty times a day, at last you come to believe it? Some men have come to believe very unlikely statements this way: and so I do not wonder that the good Spirit often blesses the method of hearing the truth often, and uses it to work faith in what is to be believed. It is written, “Faith comes by hearing,” so hear often. If I hear the gospel earnestly and attentively, one of these days I will find myself believing what I hear, through the blessed working of the Spirit of God on my mind. Only make sure that you hear the gospel, and do not distract your mind by hearing or reading what is meant to shake you.

If that, however, should seem poor advice, I would add next, consider the testimony of others. The Samaritans believed because of what the woman told them about Jesus. Many of our beliefs arise from the testimony of others. I believe that there is such a country as Japan: I have never seen it, and yet I believe that there is such a place because others have been there. I believe that I will die: I have never died, but a great many whom I once knew have done so, and therefore I am sure that I will die too; the testimony of many convinces me of that fact. Listen, then, to those who tell you how they were saved, how they were pardoned, how they were changed in character. If you look into the matter, you will find that somebody just like yourself has been saved. If you have been a thief, you will find that a thief rejoiced to wash away his sin in the fountain of Christ’s blood. If, sadly, you have been unchaste, you will find that men and women who have fallen in that way have been cleansed and changed. If you are in despair, you have only to get among God’s people and ask around a little, and you will find that some of the saints have been in as much despair as you are, and they will be pleased to tell you how the Lord delivered them. As you listen to one after another of those who have tested the word of God and found it true, the divine Spirit will lead you to believe. Have you not heard of the African who was told by the missionary that water sometimes became so hard that a man could walk on it? He declared that he believed a great many things the missionary had told him; but he would never believe that. When he came to England, it happened that one frosty day he saw the river frozen, but he would not venture onto it. He knew that it was a deep river, and he felt certain that he would drown if he ventured onto it. He could not be brought to walk on the frozen water till his friend and many others went onto it: then he was persuaded, and trusted himself where others had safely ventured. So, perhaps, as you see others believe in the Lamb of God, and notice their joy and peace, you will yourself be gently led to believe. The experience of others is one of God’s ways of helping us to faith. However that may be, you must either believe in Jesus or die; there is no hope for you but in him.

A better plan still is this — note the authority on which you are commanded to believe, and this will greatly help you to faith. The authority is not mine, or you might well reject it. It is not even the Pope’s, or you might question it. But you are commanded to believe on the authority of God himself. He tells you to believe in Jesus Christ, and you must not refuse to obey your Maker. The foreman of a certain factory in the North had often heard the Gospel, but he was troubled by the fear that he had no right to come to Christ. His good master one day sent a card around the factory — “Come to my house immediately after work.” The foreman appeared at his master’s door, and the master came out and said rather roughly, “What do you want, John, troubling me at this hour? Work is done; what right have you to be here?” “Sir,” he said, “I had a card from you saying that I was to come after work.” “Do you mean to say that just because you had a card from me you may come up to my house and call me out after business hours?” “Well, sir,” replied the foreman, “I do not understand you, but it seems to me that, as you sent for me, I had a right to come.” “Come in, John,” said his master, “I have another message I want to read to you”; and he sat down and read these words: “Come to Me, all you+ who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you+ rest.” “Do you think, after such a message from Christ, that you can be wrong in coming to him?” The poor man saw it all at once, and believed in the Lord Jesus to eternal life, because he saw that he had good warrant and authority for believing. So do you, poor soul! You have good authority for coming to Christ, for the Lord himself tells you to trust him.

If that does not breed faith in you, think over what it is that you have to believe — that the Lord Jesus Christ suffered in the place and stead of sinners, and is able to save all who trust him. Why, this is the most blessed fact that men were ever told to believe; the most suitable, the most comforting, the most divine truth that was ever set before mortal minds. I advise you to think much about it, and search out the grace and love it contains. Study the four Gospels, study Paul’s letters, and then see if the message is not so credible that you are forced to believe it.

If that does not work, then think about the person of Jesus Christ — think of who he is, and what he did, and where he is, and what he is. How can you doubt him? It is cruel to distrust the ever truthful Jesus. He has done nothing to deserve distrust; on the contrary, it should be easy to rely on him. Why crucify him again by unbelief? Is this not crowning him with thorns again, and spitting on him again? What! Is he not to be trusted? What worse insult did the soldiers heap on him than this? They made him a martyr; but you make him a liar — this is far worse. Do not ask, How can I believe? But answer another question — How can you disbelieve?

If none of these things helps, then there is something wrong with you altogether, and my last word is, submit yourself to God! Prejudice or pride lies at the bottom of this unbelief. May the Spirit of God take away your enmity and make you yield. You are a rebel, a proud rebel, and that is why you do not believe your God. Give up your rebellion; throw down your weapons; yield without conditions; surrender to your King. I believe that no soul ever threw up its hands in self-despair and cried, “Lord, I yield,” without finding that faith soon became easy to it. It is because you still have a quarrel with God, and are determined to have your own will and your own way, that you cannot believe. “How can you+ believe,” said Christ, “if you+ accept glory from one another?” Proud self creates unbelief. Submit, O man. Yield to your God, and then you will sweetly believe in your Savior. May the Holy Spirit now work secretly but effectually with you, and bring you at this very moment to believe in the Lord Jesus! Amen.

Regeneration And The Holy Spirit

“You+ must be born again.” These words of our Lord Jesus have seemed to many to flame across their path, like the drawn sword of the cherub at the gate of Paradise. They have despaired, because this change is beyond their utmost effort. The new birth is from above, and so it is not in any creature’s power. Now, I am far from wanting to deny, or even to hide, a truth in order to create a false comfort. I freely admit that the new birth is supernatural, and that the sinner cannot bring it about by himself. It would be poor help to my reader if I were wicked enough to try to cheer him by persuading him to reject or forget what is unquestionably true.

But is it not remarkable that the very chapter in which our Lord makes this sweeping declaration also contains the most explicit statement about salvation by faith? Read the third chapter of John’s gospel all the way through, and do not dwell only on its earlier sentences. It is true that the third verse reads:

““Jesus replied, ‘Truly, truly, I tell you, unless a man is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.’””

But then the fourteenth and fifteenth verses say this to us:

““Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that whoever believes in Him should not perish, but have eternal life.””

The eighteenth verse repeats the same delightful doctrine in the broadest terms:

““Whoever believes in Him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe has already been condemned, because he has not believed in the name of God’s one and only Son.””

It is clear to every reader that these two statements must agree, since they came from the same lips and are recorded on the same inspired page. Why should we make a difficulty where there can be none? If one statement assures us that something which only God can give is necessary to salvation, and another assures us that the Lord will save us when we believe in Jesus, then we may safely conclude that the Lord will give to those who believe all that is declared to be necessary to salvation. The Lord does, in fact, bring about the new birth in all who believe in Jesus; and their believing is the surest evidence that they are born again.

We trust in Jesus for what we cannot do ourselves: if it were in our own power, why would we need to look to him? It is ours to believe; it is the Lord’s to create us anew. He will not believe for us, nor are we to do the work of regeneration for him. It is enough for us to obey the gracious command; it is for the Lord to work the new birth in us. He who could go so far as to die on the cross for us can and will give us everything that is needed for our eternal safety.

“But a saving change of heart is the work of the Holy Spirit.” This too is most true, and far be it from us to question it or to forget it. But the work of the Holy Spirit is secret and mysterious, and it can be perceived only by its results. There are mysteries about our natural birth into which it would be an unholy curiosity to pry: still more is this so with the sacred workings of the Spirit of God. “The wind blows where it wishes. You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going. So it is with everyone born of the Spirit.” This much, however, we do know: the mysterious work of the Holy Spirit cannot be a reason for refusing to believe in Jesus, to whom that same Spirit bears witness.

If a man were told to sow a field, he could not excuse his neglect by saying that it would be useless to sow unless God made the seed grow. He would not be justified in neglecting to till the ground because the secret energy of God alone can create a harvest. No one is held back in the ordinary pursuits of life by the fact that unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. It is certain that no man who believes in Jesus will ever find that the Holy Spirit refuses to work in him: in fact, his believing is the proof that the Spirit is already at work in his heart.

God works in providence, but men do not therefore sit still. They could not move unless the divine power gave them life and strength, and yet they go on their way without question, the power being given from day to day by him who holds their breath in his hand, and to whom all their ways belong. So it is in grace. We repent and believe, though we could do neither if the Lord did not enable us. We forsake sin and trust in Jesus, and then we see that the Lord has worked in us to will and to do according to his good pleasure. It is idle to claim that there is any real difficulty in the matter.

Some truths that are hard to explain in words are simple enough in actual experience. There is no contradiction between the truth that the sinner believes and the truth that his faith is worked in him by the Holy Spirit. Only folly can lead men to puzzle over plain matters while their souls are in danger. No man would refuse to get into a lifeboat because he did not know the specific gravity of objects; nor would a starving man refuse to eat till he understood the whole process of nutrition. If you, my reader, will not believe till you can understand all mysteries, you will never be saved at all; and if you let difficulties of your own invention keep you from accepting pardon through your Lord and Savior, you will perish under a condemnation that will be richly deserved. Do not commit spiritual suicide through a passion for discussing metaphysical subtleties.

“My Redeemer Lives”

Again and again I have spoken to the reader about Christ crucified, who is the great hope of the guilty; but it is wise for us to remember that our Lord has risen from the dead and lives eternally.

You are not asked to trust in a dead Jesus, but in one who, though he died for our sins, has risen again for our justification. You may go to Jesus at once as to a living friend who is present with you. He is not a mere memory, but an ever-living person who will hear your prayers and answer them. He lives for the very purpose of carrying on the work for which he once laid down his life. He is interceding for sinners at the right hand of the Father, and for this reason he is able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through him. Come and try this living Savior, if you have never done so before.

This living Jesus is also raised to a height of glory and power. He does not now sorrow as “a humble man before his foes,” nor labor as “the carpenter’s son”; but he is exalted far above principalities and powers and every name that is named. The Father has given him all power in heaven and on earth, and he uses this high endowment in carrying out his work of grace. Hear what Peter and the other apostles testified about him before the high priest and the council:

““The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you+ had killed by hanging Him on a tree. God exalted Him to His right hand to be a Prince and a Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins.” — Acts 5:30, 31.”

The glory that surrounds the ascended Lord should breathe hope into every believer’s heart. Jesus is no ordinary person — he is “a Savior and a great one.” He is the crowned and enthroned Redeemer of men. The sovereign right of life and death is vested in him; the Father has put all men under the mediatorial rule of the Son, so that he can give life to whom he will. He opens, and no man shuts. At his word the soul that is bound by the cords of sin and condemnation can be set free in a moment. He stretches out the silver scepter, and whoever touches it lives.

It is well for us that as sin lives, and the flesh lives, and the devil lives, so Jesus lives; and it is also well that whatever might these may have to ruin us, Jesus has still greater power to save us.

All his exaltation and ability are for our sake. “He is exalted to be,” and exalted “to give.” He is exalted to be a Prince and a Savior, so that he may give all that is needed to accomplish the salvation of all who come under his rule. Jesus has nothing that he will not use for a sinner’s salvation, and he is nothing that he will not display in the overflowing of his grace. He links his princedom with his Saviorship, as if he would not have the one without the other; and he presents his exaltation as designed to bring blessings to men, as if this were the flower and crown of his glory. Could anything be more calculated to raise the hopes of seeking sinners who are looking to Christ?

Jesus endured great humiliation, and so there was room for him to be exalted. By that humiliation he accomplished and endured all the Father’s will, and so he was rewarded by being raised to glory. He uses that exaltation on behalf of his people. Let my reader lift his eyes to these hills of glory, from which his help must come. Let him gaze on the high glories of the Prince and Savior. Is it not most hopeful for men that a man is now on the throne of the universe? Is it not glorious that the Lord of all is the Savior of sinners? We have a friend at court; yes, a friend on the throne. He will use all his influence for those who place their affairs in his hands. As one of our poets sings so well:

““He ever lives to intercede

Before his Father’s face;

Give him, my soul, thy cause to plead,

Nor doubt the Father’s grace.””

Come, friend, and commit your cause and your case to those once-pierced hands, which are now glorified with the signet rings of royal power and honor. No case ever failed that was entrusted to this great Advocate.

Repentance Must Go With Forgiveness

It is clear from the text we have just quoted that repentance is bound up with the forgiveness of sins. In Acts 5:31 we read that Jesus is “exalted to give repentance and forgiveness of sins.” These two blessings come from that sacred hand which was once nailed to the tree, but is now raised to glory. Repentance and forgiveness are riveted together by the eternal purpose of God. What God has joined together, let no man separate.

Repentance must go with remission, and you will see that it is so if you think about the matter a little. Pardon of sin cannot be given to an impenitent sinner; that would confirm him in his evil ways, and teach him to think little of evil. If the Lord were to say, “You love sin, and live in it, and you are going from bad to worse, but all the same, I forgive you,” that would proclaim a horrible license for iniquity. The foundations of social order would be removed, and moral anarchy would follow. I cannot tell what countless evils would certainly follow if you could separate repentance and forgiveness, and overlook the sin while the sinner remained as fond of it as ever. In the very nature of things, if we believe in the holiness of God, it must be so: if we continue in our sin, and will not repent of it, we cannot be forgiven, but must reap the consequences of our stubbornness. In the infinite goodness of God, we are promised that if we will forsake our sins, confessing them, and will by faith accept the grace provided in Christ Jesus, God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. But as long as God lives, there can be no promise of mercy to those who continue in their evil ways, and refuse to acknowledge their wrongdoing. Surely no rebel can expect the King to pardon his treason while he remains in open revolt. No one can be so foolish as to imagine that the Judge of all the earth will put away our sins if we refuse to put them away ourselves.

Moreover, it must be so for the completeness of divine mercy. A mercy that could forgive the sin and yet let the sinner live in it would be a thin and shallow mercy. It would be a lopsided and deformed mercy, lame in one of its feet, and withered in one of its hands. Which do you think is the greater privilege: cleansing from the guilt of sin, or deliverance from the power of sin? I will not try to weigh in the scales two mercies so surpassing. Neither of them could have come to us apart from the precious blood of Jesus. But it seems to me that to be delivered from the dominion of sin, to be made holy, to be made like God, must be counted the greater of the two, if a comparison has to be drawn. To be forgiven is an immeasurable favor. We make this one of the first notes of our psalm of praise: “He who forgives all your iniquities.” But if we could be forgiven, and then be permitted to love sin, to run riot in iniquity, and to wallow in lust, what would be the use of such a forgiveness? Might it not turn out to be a poisoned sweet, which would most effectually destroy us? To be washed, and yet to lie in the mud; to be pronounced clean, and yet to have the leprosy white on one’s brow, would be the sheerest mockery of mercy. What good is it to bring the man out of his tomb if you leave him dead? Why lead him into the light if he is still blind? We thank God that he who forgives our iniquities also heals our diseases. He who washes us from the stains of the past also lifts us out of the foul ways of the present, and keeps us from falling in the future. We must joyfully accept both repentance and remission; they cannot be separated. The inheritance of the covenant is one and indivisible, and must not be parceled out. To divide the work of grace would be to cut the living child in two, and those who would allow this have no real claim to it.

I will ask you who are seeking the Lord: would you be satisfied with one of these mercies alone? Would it content you, my reader, if God forgave your sin and then allowed you to be as worldly and wicked as before? Oh, no: the spirit made alive is more afraid of sin itself than of its penalty. The cry of your heart is not, “Who will rescue me from punishment?” but, “What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? Who will enable me to live above temptation, and to become holy, even as God is holy?” Since the union of repentance with remission agrees with the desires of a gracious heart, and since it is necessary for the completeness of salvation, and for holiness’ sake, you may rest assured that it stands.

Repentance and forgiveness are joined together in the experience of all believers. There never yet was a person who sincerely repented of sin with believing repentance who was not forgiven; and on the other hand, there never was a person forgiven who had not repented of his sin. I do not hesitate to say that under the vault of heaven there never was, there is not, and there never will be, any case of sin being washed away, unless at the same time the heart was led to repentance and faith in Christ. Hatred of sin and a sense of pardon come into the soul together, and remain together as long as we live.

These two things act and react on each other: the man who is forgiven therefore repents; and the man who repents is also most certainly forgiven. Remember first that forgiveness leads to repentance. As we sing in Hart’s words:

““Law and terrors do but harden,

All the while they work alone;

But a sense of blood-bought pardon

Soon dissolves a heart of stone.””

When we are sure that we are forgiven, then we abhor iniquity; and I suppose that when faith grows into full assurance, so that we are certain beyond a doubt that the blood of Jesus has washed us whiter than snow, it is then that repentance reaches its greatest height. Repentance grows as faith grows. Make no mistake about it: repentance is not a thing of days and weeks, a temporary penance to be gotten over as fast as possible! No; it is the grace of a lifetime, like faith itself. God’s little children repent, and so do the young men and the fathers. Repentance is the inseparable companion of faith. All the while that we walk by faith and not by sight, the tear of repentance glistens in the eye of faith. That is not true repentance which does not come from faith in Jesus, and that is not true faith in Jesus which is not tinged with repentance. Faith and repentance, like conjoined twins, are joined together in one life. The more we believe in the forgiving love of Christ, the more we repent; and the more we repent of sin and hate evil, the more we rejoice in the fullness of the absolution which Jesus is exalted to give. You will never value pardon unless you feel repentance; and you will never taste repentance at its deepest until you know that you are pardoned. It may seem a strange thing, but so it is — the bitterness of repentance and the sweetness of pardon blend in the flavor of every gracious life, and make up an incomparable happiness.

These two covenant gifts assure us of each other. If I know that I repent, I know that I am forgiven. How am I to know that I am forgiven unless I also know that I have turned from my former sinful course? To be a believer is to be a penitent. Faith and repentance are only two spokes in the same wheel, two handles of the same plow. Repentance has been well described as a heart broken for sin, and from sin; and it may just as well be spoken of as turning and returning. It is a change of mind of the most thorough and radical kind, and it comes with sorrow for the past and a resolve to do better in the future.

““Repentance is to leave

The sins we loved before;

And show that we in earnest grieve,

By doing so no more.””

Now, when that is so, we may be certain that we are forgiven; for the Lord never made a heart to be broken for sin and broken from sin without pardoning it. If, on the other hand, we are enjoying pardon through the blood of Jesus, and are justified by faith, and have peace with God through Jesus Christ our Lord, we know that our repentance and faith are of the right kind.

Do not regard your repentance as the cause of your remission, but as its companion. Do not expect to be able to repent until you see the grace of our Lord Jesus, and his readiness to blot out your sin. Keep these blessed things in their places, and see them in their relation to each other. They are the Jachin and Boaz of a saving experience; I mean that they are like Solomon’s two great pillars which stood at the front of the house of the Lord, and formed a majestic entrance to the holy place. No man comes to God rightly unless he passes between the pillars of repentance and remission. The rainbow of covenant grace has been displayed on your heart in all its beauty when the light of full forgiveness has shone on the teardrops of repentance. Repentance of sin and faith in divine pardon are the warp and woof of the fabric of real conversion. By these marks you will know a true Israelite.

To come back to the Scripture we are meditating on: both forgiveness and repentance flow from the same source, and are given by the same Savior. The Lord Jesus in his glory gives both to the same people. You are not to find either the remission or the repentance anywhere else. Jesus has both ready, and he is prepared to give them now, and to give them most freely to all who will accept them from his hands. Let it never be forgotten that Jesus gives all that is needed for our salvation. It is highly important that all who seek mercy should remember this. Faith is as much the gift of God as is the Savior on whom that faith relies. Repentance of sin is as truly the work of grace as the making of an atonement by which sin is blotted out. Salvation, from first to last, is of grace alone. You will not misunderstand me. It is not the Holy Spirit who repents. He has never done anything for which he should repent. If he could repent, it would not meet the case; we must repent of our own sin ourselves, or we are not saved from its power. It is not the Lord Jesus Christ who repents. What should he repent of? We ourselves repent with the full consent of every faculty of our mind. The will, the affections, the emotions, all work together most heartily in the blessed act of repentance for sin; and yet behind all that is our personal act there is a secret, holy influence which melts the heart, gives contrition, and produces a complete change. The Spirit of God enlightens us to see what sin is, and so makes it loathsome in our eyes. The Spirit of God also turns us toward holiness, makes us heartily appreciate, love, and desire it, and so gives us the impulse by which we are led on from stage to stage of sanctification. The Spirit of God works in us to will and to do according to God’s good pleasure. To that good Spirit let us submit ourselves at once, that he may lead us to Jesus, who will freely give us the double blessing of repentance and remission, according to the riches of his grace.

“By grace you+ have been saved.”

How Repentance Is Given

To return to the great text: “God exalted Him to His right hand to be a Prince and a Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins.” Our Lord Jesus Christ has gone up so that grace may come down. His glory is used to spread his grace more widely. The Lord has not taken one step upward except with the purpose of carrying believing sinners upward with him. He is exalted to give repentance; and we will see this if we remember a few great truths.

The work our Lord Jesus has done has made repentance possible, available, and acceptable. The law makes no mention of repentance, but says plainly, “The soul who sins is the one who will die.” If the Lord Jesus had not died and risen again and gone to the Father, what would your repenting or mine be worth? We might feel remorse with its horrors, but never repentance with its hopes. Repentance, as a natural feeling, is a common duty that deserves no great praise: indeed, it is so generally mixed with a selfish fear of punishment that the kindest estimate makes little of it. If Jesus had not stepped in and worked out a wealth of merit, our tears of repentance would have been so much water spilled on the ground. Jesus is exalted on high, so that through the power of his intercession repentance may have a place before God. In this respect he gives us repentance, because he puts repentance in a position of acceptance which it could never otherwise have held.

When Jesus was exalted on high, the Spirit of God was poured out to work in us all the graces we need. The Holy Spirit creates repentance in us by renewing our nature supernaturally, and taking away the heart of stone out of our flesh. Oh, do not sit straining those eyeballs of yours to force out impossible tears; repentance does not come from unwilling nature, but from free and sovereign grace. Do not go to your room and beat your breast in order to draw out of a heart of stone feelings which are not there. But go to Calvary and see how Jesus died. Look up to the hills from which your help comes. The Holy Spirit has come for the very purpose of overshadowing men’s spirits and breeding repentance within them, just as he once brooded over chaos and brought order out of it. Breathe your prayer to him, “Blessed Spirit, dwell with me. Make me tender and lowly of heart, that I may hate sin and sincerely repent of it.” He will hear your cry and answer you.

Remember, too, that when our Lord Jesus was exalted, he gave us repentance not only by sending the Holy Spirit, but by consecrating all the works of nature and of providence to the great purposes of our salvation, so that any one of them may call us to repentance, whether it crows like Peter’s rooster, or shakes the prison like the jailer’s earthquake. From the right hand of God our Lord Jesus rules all things here below, and makes them work together for the salvation of his redeemed. He uses both bitter things and sweet, trials and joys, to produce in sinners a better mind toward their God. Be thankful for the providence which has made you poor, or sick, or sad; for by all this Jesus works the life of your spirit and turns you to himself. The Lord’s mercy often rides to the door of our hearts on the black horse of affliction. Jesus uses the whole range of our experience to wean us from earth and woo us to heaven. Christ is exalted to the throne of heaven and earth so that, by all the workings of his providence, he may bring hard hearts under the gracious softening of repentance.

Besides, he is at work at this very hour by all his whispers in the conscience, by his inspired Book, by those of us who speak out of that Book, and by praying friends and earnest hearts. He can send you a word which will strike your rocky heart as with the rod of Moses, and make streams of repentance flow. He can bring to your mind some heartbreaking text of Holy Scripture which will conquer you very quickly. He can mysteriously soften you, and cause a holy frame of mind to steal over you when you least expect it. Be sure of this: he who has gone into his glory, raised into all the splendor and majesty of God, has abundant ways of working repentance in those to whom he grants forgiveness. He is even now waiting to give repentance to you. Ask him for it at once.

Notice, to your great comfort, that the Lord Jesus Christ gives this repentance to the most unlikely people in the world. He is exalted to give repentance to Israel. To Israel! In the days when the apostles spoke this way, Israel was the nation which had most grossly sinned against light and love, and had crowned its guilt by crucifying the Lord, and daring to say, “His blood be on us and on our children!” Why, these were the murderers of Jesus; and yet he is exalted to give them repentance! What a marvel of grace! Listen, then. If you have been brought up in the brightest Christian light, and yet have rejected it, there is still hope. If you have sinned against conscience, and against the Holy Spirit, and against the love of Jesus, there is still room for repentance. Though you may be as hard as unbelieving Israel of old, softening may yet come to you, since Jesus is exalted, and clothed with boundless power. For those who went furthest in iniquity, and sinned with especially aggravated guilt, the Lord Jesus is exalted to give them repentance and forgiveness of sins. How happy I am to have so full a gospel to proclaim! How happy you are to be allowed to hear it!

The hearts of the children of Israel had grown as hard as flint. Luther used to think it impossible to convert a Jew. We are far from agreeing with him, and yet we must admit that the people of Israel have been exceedingly obstinate in rejecting the Savior through these many centuries. Truly the Lord said, “Israel would have none of Me.” “He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him.” Yet on behalf of Israel our Lord Jesus is exalted to give repentance and remission. My reader is probably a Gentile; but he may still have a very stubborn heart, which has held out against the Lord Jesus for many years; and yet our Lord can work repentance in him. It may be that you too will one day feel compelled to write as William Hone did when he yielded to divine love. He was the author of those most entertaining volumes called the “Every-day Book,” but he was once a stubborn unbeliever. When he was subdued by sovereign grace, he wrote:

““The proudest heart that ever beat

Hath been subdued in me;

The wildest will that ever rose

To scorn thy cause and aid thy foes

Is quell’d, my Lord, by thee.”

““Thy will, and not my will be done,

My heart be ever thine;

Confessing thee the mighty Word,

My Savior Christ, my God, my Lord,

Thy cross shall be my sign.””

The Lord can give repentance to the most unlikely, turning lions into lambs, and ravens into doves. Let us seek him, that this great change may be worked in us. Certainly, thinking about the death of Christ is one of the surest and quickest ways of gaining repentance. Do not sit down and try to pump up repentance from the dry well of corrupt nature. It is against the laws of the mind to suppose that you can force your soul into that gracious state. Take your heart in prayer to him who understands it, and say, “Lord, cleanse it. Lord, renew it. Lord, work repentance in it.” The more you try to produce feelings of penitence in yourself, the more you will be disappointed; but if, believing, you think of Jesus dying for you, repentance will burst out. Meditate on the Lord’s shedding his heart’s blood out of love for you. Set before your mind’s eye the agony and bloody sweat, the cross and suffering; and, as you do this, he who bore all this grief will look at you, and with that look he will do for you what he did for Peter, so that you also will go out and weep bitterly. He who died for you can, by his gracious Spirit, make you die to sin; and he who has gone into glory on your behalf can draw your soul after him, away from evil, and toward holiness.

I will be content if I leave this one thought with you: do not look under the ice to find fire, nor hope to find repentance in your own natural heart. Look to the Living One for life. Look to Jesus for all you need between Hell Gate and Heaven Gate. Never look anywhere else for any part of what Jesus loves to give; but remember,

Christ is all.

The Fear Of Final Falling

A dark fear haunts the minds of many who are coming to Christ; they are afraid that they will not persevere to the end. I have heard the seeker say: “If I were to cast my soul on Jesus, perhaps I would still draw back to destruction after all. I have had good feelings before now, and they have died away. My goodness has been like the morning cloud, and like the early dew. It has come all of a sudden, lasted for a while, promised much, and then vanished away.”

My reader, I believe that this fear is often the father of the fact; and that some who have been afraid to trust Christ for all time, and for all eternity, have failed because they had a temporary faith, which never went far enough to save them. They set out trusting Jesus to some extent, but looking to themselves to keep going and to persevere on the way to heaven; and so they set out on the wrong footing, and, as a natural consequence, turned back before long. If we trust ourselves for our holding on, we will not hold on. Even if we rest on Jesus for part of our salvation, we will fail if we trust self for anything. No chain is stronger than its weakest link: if Jesus is our hope for everything except one thing, we will utterly fail, because at that one point we will come to nothing. I have no doubt whatever that a mistake about the perseverance of the saints has prevented the perseverance of many who were running well. What hindered them from continuing to run? They trusted themselves for that running, and so they stopped short. Beware of mixing even a little of self into the mortar you build with, or you will make it poorly mixed mortar, and the stones will not hold together. If you look to Christ for your beginnings, beware of looking to yourself for your endings. He is Alpha. See to it that you make him Omega too. If you begin in the Spirit, you must not hope to be made perfect by the flesh. Begin as you mean to go on, and go on as you began, and let the Lord be all in all to you. Oh, that God the Holy Spirit may give us a very clear idea of where the strength must come from by which we will be preserved until the day of our Lord’s appearing!

Here is what Paul once said on this subject when he was writing to the Corinthians:

““Our Lord Jesus Christ, who will also confirm you+ to the end, so that you+ will be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is faithful, by whom you+ were called into the fellowship of His Son Jesus Christ our Lord.” — 1 Cor 1:8, 9.”

This language quietly admits a great need, by telling us how it is met. Wherever the Lord makes a provision, we may be quite sure that there was a need for it, since nothing superfluous clutters the covenant of grace. Golden shields hung in Solomon’s courts which were never used, but there are none like them in the armory of God. What God has provided we will surely need. Between this hour and the end of all things, every promise of God and every provision of the covenant of grace will be called into use. The urgent need of the believing soul is confirmation, continuance, final perseverance, preservation to the end. This is the great need of the most advanced believers, for Paul was writing to saints at Corinth, who were men of a high order, of whom he could say, “I always thank my God for you+ because of the grace He has given you+ in Christ Jesus.” Such men are the very people who most surely feel that they need new grace every day if they are to hold on, and hold out, and come off conquerors at the last. If you+ were not saints you+ would have no grace, and you+ would feel no need of more grace; but because you+ are men of God, you+ feel the daily demands of the spiritual life. The marble statue needs no food; but the living man hungers and thirsts, and he rejoices that his bread and his water are made sure to him, for otherwise he would certainly faint on the way. The believer’s personal needs make it inevitable that he should draw daily from the great source of all supplies; for what could he do if he could not turn to his God?

This is true of the most gifted of the saints — of those men at Corinth who were enriched in all speech and in all knowledge. They needed to be confirmed to the end, or else their gifts and attainments would prove their ruin. If we had the tongues of men and of angels, where would we be if we did not receive fresh grace? If we had every experience, till we were fathers in the church — if we had been taught by God so as to understand all mysteries — we still could not live a single day without the divine life flowing into us from our Covenant Head. How could we hope to hold on for a single hour, to say nothing of a lifetime, unless the Lord held us on? He who began the good work in us must complete it until the day of Christ, or it will prove a painful failure.

This great need arises very largely from ourselves. Some have a painful fear that they will not persevere in grace, because they know their own fickleness. Certain people are unstable by temperament. Some men are by nature conservative, not to say obstinate; but others are just as naturally changeable and volatile. Like butterflies, they flit from flower to flower, till they have visited all the beauties of the garden, and settle on none of them. They never stay long enough in one place to do any good; not even in their business nor in their intellectual pursuits. Such people may well be afraid that ten, twenty, thirty, forty, perhaps fifty years of continual religious watchfulness will be far too much for them. We see men joining first one church and then another, till they have gone all around the compass. They are everything by turns and nothing for long. Such people have double need to pray that they may be confirmed by God, and made not only steadfast but immovable, or else they will not be found “always abounding in the work of the Lord.”

All of us, even if we have no temptation to fickleness in our temperament, must feel our own weakness if we have really been made alive by God. Dear reader, do you not find enough in any single day to make you stumble? You+ who desire to walk in perfect holiness, as I trust you+ do; you+ who have set before you+ a high standard of what a Christian should be — do you+ not find that before the breakfast things are cleared from the table, you+ have shown enough folly to make you+ ashamed of yourselves+? If we were to shut ourselves up in a hermit’s lonely cell, temptation would follow us; for as long as we cannot escape from ourselves, we cannot escape from incitements to sin. There is something in our hearts which should make us watchful and humble before God. If he does not confirm us, we are so weak that we will stumble and fall; not overturned by an enemy, but by our own carelessness. Lord, be our strength. We are weakness itself.

Besides that, there is the weariness which comes from a long life. When we first profess our faith in Christ, we mount up with wings like eagles; further on we run without growing weary; but in our best and truest days we walk without fainting. Our pace seems slower, but it is more useful and better sustained. I pray God that the energy of our youth may stay with us, so far as it is the energy of the Spirit and not the mere fermentation of proud flesh. He who has long been on the road to heaven finds that there was good reason why it was promised that his shoes would be iron and brass, for the road is rough. He has found out that there are Hills of Difficulty and Valleys of Humiliation; that there is a Vale of Deathshade, and, worse still, a Vanity Fair — and all these must be passed through. If there are Delectable Mountains (and, thank God, there are), there are also Castles of Despair, whose insides pilgrims have too often seen. All things considered, those who hold out to the end in the way of holiness will be “men wondered at.”

“O world of wonders, I can say no less.” The days of a Christian’s life are like so many Koh-i-noor diamonds of mercy threaded on the golden string of divine faithfulness. In heaven we will tell angels, and principalities, and powers of the unsearchable riches of Christ which were spent on us, and enjoyed by us while we were here below. We have been kept alive on the brink of death. Our spiritual life has been a flame burning on in the middle of the sea, a stone that has stayed hanging in the air. It will amaze the universe to see us enter the pearly gate, blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. We ought to be full of grateful wonder if we are kept for an hour; and I trust we are.

If this were all, there would be cause enough for anxiety; but there is far more. We have to think of what a place we live in. The world is a howling wilderness to many of God’s people. Some of us are greatly favored in the providence of God, but others have a hard fight of it. We begin our day with prayer, and we hear the sound of holy song very often in our homes; but many good people have hardly risen from their knees in the morning before they are greeted with blasphemy. They go out to work, and all day long they are vexed with filthy conversation, like righteous Lot in Sodom. Can you even walk the open streets these days without your ears being afflicted by foul language? The world is no friend to grace. The best we can do with this world is to get through it as quickly as we can, for we live in an enemy’s country. A robber lurks in every bush. Everywhere we need to travel with a drawn sword in our hand, or at least with that weapon which is called all-prayer always at our side; for we have to fight for every inch of our way. Make no mistake about this, or you will be roughly shaken out of your fond delusion. O God, help us, and confirm us to the end, or where will we be?

True religion is supernatural at its beginning, supernatural in its continuance, and supernatural at its close. It is the work of God from first to last. There is great need that the hand of the Lord should still be stretched out: my reader is feeling that need now, and I am glad that he feels it; for now he will look for his own preservation to the Lord, who alone is able to keep us from falling, and to glorify us with his Son.

Confirmation

I want you to notice the security which Paul confidently expected for all the saints. He says, “Who will confirm you+ to the end, so that you+ will be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.” This is the kind of confirmation which is to be desired above all things. You see, it assumes that the people are in the right, and it sets out to confirm them in the right. It would be an awful thing to confirm a man in ways of sin and error. Think of a confirmed drunkard, or a confirmed thief, or a confirmed liar. It would be a deplorable thing for a man to be confirmed in unbelief and ungodliness. Divine confirmation can be enjoyed only by those to whom the grace of God has already been shown. It is the work of the Holy Spirit. He who gives faith strengthens and establishes it: he who kindles love in us preserves it and increases its flame. What he makes us know by his first teaching, the good Spirit causes us to know with greater clearness and certainty by still further instruction. Holy acts are confirmed till they become habits, and holy feelings are confirmed till they become settled states. Experience and practice confirm our beliefs and our resolutions. Both our joys and our sorrows, our successes and our failures, are sanctified to the very same end; just as the tree is helped to root itself both by the soft showers and by the rough winds. The mind is instructed, and in its growing knowledge it gathers reasons for persevering in the good way: the heart is comforted, and so it is made to cling more closely to the consoling truth. The grip grows tighter, and the step grows firmer, and the man himself becomes more solid and substantial.

This is not a merely natural growth, but is as distinct a work of the Spirit as conversion. The Lord will surely give it to those who are relying on him for eternal life.
